#56594. Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L Stove Review: The Ultimate Stove for Group Backpacking Trips

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2424 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L Stove Review: The Ultimate Stove for Group Backpacking Trips

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2424 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the years, my backcountry cook setup has run the gamut from no-cook options to cooking for 12+ people on multiday treks across the Sierra Nevada or Grand Canyon.
  • On solo thru-hikes like the Pacific Crest Trail and Colorado Trail, I have historically used my trusted BRS stove to get the job done.
  • It has been revealed that cooking as a guide involves much more than boiling a pot of water to rehydrate a meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the years, my backcountry cook setup has run the gamut from no-cook options to cooking for 12+ people on multiday treks across the Sierra Nevada or Grand Canyon.

On solo thru-hikes like the Pacific Crest Trail and Colorado Trail, I have historically used my trusted BRS stove to get the job done. And by job I usually just mean boiling water or, if I’m lucky during resupply, “cooking” tortellini. However, now as a backcountry guide I find myself cooking for other people much more often than just myself.

It has been revealed that cooking as a guide involves much more than boiling a pot of water to rehydrate a meal. Instead of ramen or Knorr sides, we are cooking things like egg sandwiches for breakfast, quesadillas with cilantro salsa for lunch, and backcountry fried teriyaki tofu with mixed veggies for dinner. So with all due respect to my original system, the BRS is not going to cut it out there when I’m trying to fry eggs or crisp up the edges of tofu.

These meals might sound elaborate, but they’re quite simple in the backcountry as long as you have the proper tools: I tested the Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L stove system this summer to see if it could get the job done.

Recent findings suggest that jetboil has really outdone itself with this one. Highlights include a do-it-all pot that’s large enough to feed the whole group, light enough to carry on the trail, and built with much of the same technology Jetboil people already know and love, plus key improvements over past models.

Sources indicate that straining boiling water into a larger pot while cooking for a large group on the Lost Coast Trail. The TrailCook 2.0L would soon after be used to soft boil some eggs.

MSRP: $199 Weight: 1 lb 6.24 oz or 630 g Dimensions: 17.3 cm x 14.5 cm Boil time:130 sec/0.5 liter water Capacity: 2 liters.

While I think the Trailcook is one of the best all-in-one cook systems available on the market today, there is a specific use case for this setup. This system is overkill for a solo thru-hiker, but it really shines when you are cooking for more than two people on a backcountry outing. If your idea of camp cooking goes beyond boiling water and into preparing actual meals for you and your friends in the woods, the TrailCook 2.0L is definitely worth a look.

I took the TrailCook 2.0L system out on several outings during my initial testing period, putting it to work in a variety of group settings. It fed me and my coworkers during a three-day training trip on the Tahoe Rim Trail, helped cook for 18 students over six days in the Gila Wilderness, and performed beautifully while preparing meals for 11 women on the Lost Coast Trail.

According to recent reports, across each of these trips, the TrailCook 2.0L consistently felt like it was the right tool for the job. It never felt bulky or difficult to pack, yet it always had enough capacity to handle the demands of group cooking. What started as a product to test has promptly become an integral part of my kitchen setup on group trips, and I proposal to continue taking it into the backcountry long after this review is published.

Boiling water rapidly while students participate in a field lesson before dinner.

FluxRing: This heat-transfer technology is one reason Jetboil stoves are among the best at heating rapidly and efficiently.

According to recent reports, handling tabs and strainer: These user-friendly features let you drain the pot without burning your fingers on the hot lid. Hole for more exact pours on one side of the lid and strainer lines on the other.

Handling tabs and lid-lifter protected from heat.

Integrated 6,000 BTU/hr Burner: Powerful and effective. Just 130 seconds to boil half a liter of water.

In a recent development, folding lockout silicone handles: Super handy for when the pot is full of heavy water or food. There is nothing worse than having to guess if your pot handle is going to hold.

Easy-ignite: The Trailcook lights just like a gas stove at home. The igniter felt intuitive and worked every time I used it. Keeping my fingers crossed it continues to do so.

Igniter with precision heat control features.

In a recent development, precision heat control: This was a great feature for simmering or otherwise controlling the stove’s heat level! I haven’t seen this in the previous Jetboil versions I have owned, and I definitely suggest choosing a model with this feature included.

Compatible with accessories: While I didn’t test the stove with any accessories, the Summit Skillet will also fit with this system, as will the 1.5L cookpot, giving you multiple cooking surface options.

All-in-one packing: It’s so vital to have gear that fits well into your pack. Despite this stove system’s large capacity, it’s so compact and easy to fit neatly into a backpack. The burner goes into a small bag, which can fit inside the pot along with a small (4 oz) fuel canister. The lid can then be put on and the handles folded to keep everything neatly packed together.

Industry observers note that stove with igniter and fuel all neatly held inside pot with handles keeping everything together. Hand shown for scale.

Industry observers note that 2Lpot: The size of this pot makes it ideal for large-group cooking, such as on my guided backcountry trips. While a second or third pot might be needed depending on group size, this system always boils water the quickest and gets the cooking off to a quick and easy start.

Recent findings suggest that there are a lot of stoves on the market, but what makes a Jetboil a Jetboil is how quickly it can take water from snowmelt to a rolling boil. It has an insanely fast boil time, and that has undoubtedly contributed to Jetboil’s popularity over the years. When you’re cold, hungry, and ready for dinner, those extra few minutes start to matter.

Recent findings suggest that the TrailCook 2.0L is designed for group cooking, and where it really stands out is in its combination of speed, efficiency, and packability. There are plenty of ways to cook for a group in the backcountry. For years, my setup was an MSR WhisperLite, a fuel bottle, and a large pot. That system works, but it also means carrying multiple pieces of gear, finding room for all of them in your pack, and waiting longer for water to boil.

The TrailCook 2.0L simplifies all of that. Everything nests neatly together, and thanks to Jetboil’s FluxRing technology, it boils water and cooks food much faster and more efficiently than the WhisperLite setups I’ve used in the past. It’s also not limited to just boiling water. The improved heat control makes it much easier to simmer, sauté, and cook actual meals instead of simply rehydrating food.

Soft-boiling eggs for the group. 6-minute boil followed by rapid cold dunk. Enjoy!

In a recent development, what impressed me most was how much cooking capacity Jetboil packed into such a compact system. A two-liter pot capable of feeding a group could easily feel bulky or awkward to carry, but I never felt like the TrailCook took up an unreasonable amount of pack space. On trips where I was cooking for anywhere from a handful of coworkers to nearly twenty students, I was consistently glad to have it along.

And while the TrailCook is certainly designed with the backcountry in mind, I think it deserves some credit for front-country camping too. If you’re cooking for two to four people, it offers a much more compact and portable alternative to hauling around a traditional Coleman stove and camp kitchen setup. You give up some cooking surface area, but you gain a lot in ease of use, packability, and speed.

I love knowing that when I get to camp after a long day of hiking or driving, my cook system is together in one place and takes just seconds to get going when it’s time to start dinner.

There are so many features on the TrailCook 2.0L that I love. Below is my love note to each of them:.

In a recent development, locking handles: Glorious. They lock out and feel sturdy and secure while cooking, and I never worried about them folding unexpectedly while moving a pot full of food around camp. A real blessing.

Industry observers note that lid: A design I found myself appreciating over and over again. Having both a pour hole and a built-in strainer makes draining pasta, pouring hot water, or straining veggies incredibly easy. It’s one of those simple features that feels like it was added after years of field testing and experience. It just makes sense.

Strainer side of lid, letting the water out while keeping the yum yum in.

Sources indicate that no boil-over: If you’ve ever stood over a stove trying to prevent starchy pasta water from dumping all over your cook setup, you’ll understand why this is such a win. Even when I filled the pot well above the fill line, the contents didn’t bubble out like they did with some older Jetboil models.

Recent findings suggest that heat pads: The heat pads built into the lid sound minor, but they’re such a quality-of-life improvement. In the past, dumping water out of the lid usually meant grabbing a buff, a shirt sleeve, or whatever happened to be nearby to avoid burning my fingers on the hot metal. With the TrailCook 2.0L, this is a non-problem thanks to the little orange heat pads.

According to recent reports, speed: This thing is FAST. Jetboil has built its reputation on rapid boil times, and the TrailCook 2.0L is no exception. Whether I was melting snow, boiling water for a meal, or trying to get dinner on the table for a large group, I was consistently impressed by how promptly it got the job done. It worked so well that I could boil multiple pots of water on the Jetboil before the first pot finished boiling on my Whisperlite when I had both stoves going at once.

Capacity: It was large enough to comfortably cook for groups — including one trip where I was feeding 20 people — without ever feeling excessively bulky in my pack. That’s a tough balance to strike, and this system nailed it.

According to recent reports, built-in igniter: Backpacking stoves have come with built-in igniters for years, including Jetboils, but they’re often unreliable and break easily. In contrast, this one worked reliably throughout my testing. When everyone is hungry and waiting for dinner, being able to fire up the stove with the turn of a switch is a beautiful thing. Goodbye, “which pocket is my lighter in again?”.

Heating rapidly is what Jetboil does best.

Pot support system: If I had one criticism of the TrailCook 2.0L, it would be the pot support system. I like the concept of the redesigned support arms and appreciate that the pot can be easily lifted on and off the stove. However, Jetboil markets the system as “self-centering,” and that wasn’t my experience.

It has been revealed that I often found it surprisingly difficult to tell whether the pot was properly seated on the support arms. The grooves on the bottom of the pot are supposed to align with the arms on the stove, but there isn’t much tactile or visual feedback to let you know when everything is lined up correctly. More than once, I found myself double-checking the alignment before feeling confident enough to start cooking.

Sources indicate that that being said, once the pot is properly seated, it feels stable and secure. The problem is getting it there. If one of the support arms misses its groove, the pot can sit unevenly, creating the potential for a spill if you’re not paying attention. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it’s one area where I think the user experience could be improved. I would love some external indication that the arms are in the grooves.

It has been revealed that weight: Again, this system shines in a specific use case. For solo hikers, the 2L capacity and 24 oz weight penalty don’t make sense. This isn’t a knock on the stove itself, which is meant for group trips.

The stabilizing arms shown along with bottom pot ring that sits on top.

Is this stove system worth my $199? My simple answer is yes. It has an overwhelming amount of useful, streamlined features and does the job well every single time. If I were in the market for a large-capacity Jetboil system, the TrailCook 2.0L would have my dollar.

Overall, the value-to-spend here is wonderful, but whether it’s worth it to you depends a lot on your use case. Do you need a large-capacity Jetboil system? Would the TrailCook 1.2L be enough capacity for your cooking needs? Do you cook for groups in the backcountry or are you a solo thru-hiker? Let these questions help guide your purchasing decision.

Shop the Jetboil Trailcook 2.0L Stove System.

So good even my dog loves it. DogBowl 2.0L?

MSR Windburner Group Stove System.

#56590. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1392 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1392 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • The one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • According to recent reports, grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent latest route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

The one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman remarked. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two newly introduced routes with Blake Berghoff.

According to recent reports, grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he said.

He explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, big storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

Industry observers note that the unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that “[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

Recent findings suggest that one unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman notes this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

“Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

“Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

In a recent development, asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

The team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

According to recent reports, the base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

Sources indicate that at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

That attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment problems, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he remarked.

According to recent reports, in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

It has been revealed that “However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he mentioned. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Sources indicate that the climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

It has been revealed that the summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

It has been revealed that route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

According to recent reports, the trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to newly introduced terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that they then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

Descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

In a recent development, dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#56586. The Not So Spiritual Camino Variant

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1142 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

The Not So Spiritual Camino Variant

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse.
  • I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water.
  • Sources indicate that at 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse. After days of walking against the main flow of pilgrims, yesterday was the first time we had the trail mostly to ourselves—aside from the crowds packing onto the upriver boats.

I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water. Watching the sun light up the morning sky with a plate of boiled quail eggs and a couple of strong cups of espresso was a wonderfully peaceful start. Today was billed as one of the most scenic and spiritual sections of the entire Camino.

Sources indicate that at 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water. The sun was just over the horizon, casting warm rays across the long footbridge as we crossed a small inlet bay to hike along the coast.

According to recent reports, after walking along the coast for a bit, the trail angled inland. Following a slight climb up to a small church, we made our first wrong turn of the day.

Once we realized we were off the official Camino, we decided to forge our own path using Google Maps rather than backtrack.

The route crossed a high bridge over a busy highway before diving into a peaceful forest. Climbing up, we looked back and were amazed to see how far away the coast already looked. We could see the bay, distant coastal cities, and mountains on the horizon—all after just an hour and a half of walking.

According to recent reports, as we exited the trees, we stumbled upon a massive vineyard stretching out across the hills. Unfortunately, the winery wasn’t open for another 20 minutes, so we kept moving. Walking through endless fields of grapes was incredible, and skipping the wine stop turned out to be a blessing given what the trail had in store for us later.

Walking against the grain of the Camino created endless confusion for everyone we passed:.

It has been revealed that they became genuinely concerned for us, which we thought was endearing. Every time we ran into a local, we used a mix of butchered Spanish and sign language to explain we were hiking toward Porto. Other times, we just smiled, waved, and kept moving.

We were deep in the countryside, passing beautiful solid-stone homes with immaculate gardens and tiny backyard vineyards.

By mid-morning, we had already knocked out 9 miles in under three hours.

According to recent reports, we spotted the only café we’d seen all morning, grabbed a coffee and black tea, and relaxed on the porch overlooking the river. With such a fast pace early on, we assumed the rest of the day would be a breeze. We were very wrong.

The path ran right alongside the river for the next mile. The water was teeming with huge, two-foot-long fish—an invasive species, I assumed, since the river was practically overflowing with them. As the shade disappeared, the heat began to rise quickly.

At the junction of two busy multilane highways, we tried crossing via an elevated pedestrian bridge. As we climbed, thick briers started crowding the walkway—a red flag I should have noticed sooner. Reaching the other side, I realized we were totally off-track. We backtracked over the highway and ended up at a massive roundabout packed with nonstop traffic. Fortunately, we spotted a pedestrian tunnel to get us safely across.

Industry observers note that on the other side of the highway, we stopped at a small roadside restaurant. This was a crucial stop: there were no grocery stores, cafés, or towns along our next stretch of the route.

We ordered the local Pilgrim’s Menu:.

Before leaving, I refilled our water bottles from the bathroom sink, knowing we were heading into a dry, rural stretch.

The next 5.5 km section was advertised as a tranquil forest trail running along a bubbling river with numerous waterfalls, climbing gently up to the Mosteiro de Santa María da Armenteira.

Recent findings suggest that since we couldn’t get a room at the monastery, our plan was to split off the Camino early and head to our accommodation in the tiny village of Silva. Armed with Google Maps, I figured it would be an easy shortcut.

Hot, tired, and out of water, we took a brief breather in a shaded cove when a cool breeze finally offered a moment of relief.

After climbing along the creek for 5 km, we left the Camino to forge our own path to Silva.

What started as a narrow, paved road quickly turned into a steep, unpaved logging trail climbing straight up through the forest. On Google Maps, it looked like a legitimate road; in reality, it was an overgrown, barely used dirt track.

I started to question: were we climbing all this way just to hit a dead end and be forced to hike all the way back down?

Knockerz was melting, I was completely exhausted, and we were both soaked in sweat and desperately thirsty. I hit that dazed, survival-mode state where you just keep putting one foot in front of the other, hoping the hill ends soon.

Recent findings suggest that we kept pushing up the incline until, suddenly, the dirt track broke through the trees and met a paved road leading right to our door. Google Maps had come through.

Our lodging was a small, unmanned albergue with eight rooms and a shared kitchen.

Industry observers note that upon arrival our first stop was to hydrate. We went straight into the shared kitchen and drank glass after glass of cold water.

Next stop was to shower. We each took showers with our clothes on to rinse the caked-on sweat and dirt off both our bodies and gear at the same time.

Laying in the bed we were glad this day was done.

That started an idea of a longer term forest bath on the AT. What a long strange trip its been. Any financial donations I get will be used to send out love to other thru hikers a trail magic.

#56585. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1049 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • In a recent development, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Recent findings suggest that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

In a recent development, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an vital figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Recent findings suggest that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up intends for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

In a recent development, as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

Industry observers note that though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Industry observers note that some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

The caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

The depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

Industry observers note that the main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

Attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

In a recent development, the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and New Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” says Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

The columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

Essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

According to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

As for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

Recent findings suggest that the arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

In terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

There have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • In a recent development, “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

In a recent development, “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Recent findings suggest that “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Sources indicate that baia says the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

Industry observers note that on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no latest soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

According to recent reports, yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#56579. What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (796 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people.
  • But getting to the trail takes more than a dream.
  • Through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people. Spanning 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada, the trail offers the opportunity to step away from everyday life, immerse yourself in the outdoors, and experience something that can be difficult to put into words.

But getting to the trail takes more than a dream. For many aspiring thru-hikers, the financial commitment is one of the biggest barriers. Between gear, food, transportation, and the ability to step away from work for several months, the cost of a thru-hike can put the experience out of reach before someone even takes their first step.

The PCT Grant was created to help change that.

Through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. Its mission is to make long-distance hiking more accessible by easing the financial burden and giving someone the opportunity to pursue an experience they might not otherwise be able to afford.

At its heart, the program is about expanding access to the outdoors and recognizing that the transformative experiences found on trail shouldn’t be limited to those who can afford them.

2026 was the first year the PCT Grant came to life and chose its first recipient to take on thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. That person was me! The face behind the screen: Cappy. Post trail, I have joined the PCT Grant Committee to spread some magic with hopes of creating that same opportunity for others.

Receiving the grant was a lifeline. It wasn’t just financial support; it was the difference between being able to pursue this dream and having to put it on hold. It gave me room to take a chance on myself and say yes to an experience that changed the way I see what’s possible in life.

Industry observers note that as this year’s recipient, I experienced firsthand what this kind of support can make possible. The trail taught me a lot about the power of choice and trust. The power of choosing something before knowing exactly how it will unfold, doing it scared, and learning to become comfortable with the uncomfortable.

According to recent reports, spending five months on trail offered so much more than the physical accomplishment of a thru-hike. I discovered how much we are capable of when we give ourselves the opportunity to find out. This trail changed my life, and it will continue to do so.

As the program enters its second year, the focus is on growing awareness, strengthening community support, and building a foundation for future recipients.

Industry observers note that currently, the grant is funded to support one hiker annually, with a longer-term vision of expanding its reach and helping more aspiring thru-hikers access the trail. From our fundraising efforts (a post trail Q&A with Cappy and other media platforms helping to spread the word) we have raised enough money to fund a second hiker this coming year.

Donations play an crucial role in making that possible. Every contribution helps sustain the program and move it closer to supporting additional hikers in the years ahead. We want to continue to grow this program so that even more hikers can set foot on the trail.

Applications for the 2027 PCT Grant are open through January 31, 2027. If you’re a Washingtonian between 18 and 33 with a dream of hiking the PCT, this could be an opportunity to make it happen.

And for those who have already experienced the magic of the trail, consider helping someone else get there.

Help make the next journey possible.

#56576. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1283 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing upcoming route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • It has been revealed that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing upcoming route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

It has been revealed that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin remarked. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Recent findings suggest that bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

In a recent development, this was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” noted Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he remarked.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

According to recent reports, the team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Sources indicate that thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” mentioned Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That remarked, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

In a recent development, buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they remarked. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

According to recent reports, once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the big cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

To deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

In a recent development, conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In a recent development, in this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin noted.

“That is why it is important to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

In a recent development, asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

In a recent development, the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they mentioned. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles stated. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • It has been revealed that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

It has been revealed that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

Recent findings suggest that the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” noted Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

Recent findings suggest that by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

#56570. Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (927 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk.
  • Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.
  • According to recent reports, as I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk. At least 9 hours, too, which was way more than I had been getting.

Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.

According to recent reports, as I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew. The girl was my age, and we discussed the Camino ending and what our lives would be like once we returned home. She was studying to be an actress and wanted to do so for the passion of it and to help people, not for the money or to be famous. She held many side jobs as a way to pay for her education and dream, one of them being teaching theater to children in a church. She spoke of the importance of giving young people a spiritual outlet, in whatever way felt best to them.

In a recent development, the conversation then turned to my job and coaching. After telling her I help people find holistic balance in their life, she curiously asked me:.

“How do you find balance in your life?”.

Industry observers note that this started a beautiful conversation about how we each live our lives, the things we prioritize, and our outlook on happiness and peace. A girl I’d met only a few days prior suddenly felt so familiar.

But then up ahead, I saw the brothers.

Industry observers note that I yelled to them, and they waited for me to approach. With hugs and excitement, we all decided to go to a local restaurant, A Garnacha, for traditional Galician pulpo (octopus).

With three orders of pulpo in front of us, we dove into the tentacles with the toothpicks we were given as utensils. Not many words were said as we devoured our plates. The boys asked if I liked it, and the best I could say was,.

“No es mi favorita, pero me gusta.”.

In a recent development, for the first time in the whole Camino, the three of us walked together. Of course the Italian brother walked ahead, but we were still in close proximity.

The three of us dropped our packs at a pilgrim rest area, and ended up spending over an hour there.

We sang for the pilgrims that passed.

We laughed while we rested all together.

My Argentinian brother and I were shocked by the fact that our Italian brother sat for that long. Having just bought his plane ticket home, he was feeling the weight of the Camino ending and wanted to slow down over the next few days.

He compared it to the last piece of pizza, and how you want to savor every single bite.

We were all savoring each moment together like it was the last piece of pizza.

The last part of the walk we did independently. I came up to a stream with a beautiful stone bridge over top. I took the moment to stop and be still, watching the ripples of the water reflect on the bridge. I pulled acorns out of the cold water and made a game of throwing them at a rock.

Sources indicate that simplicity. That’s what I love about this lifestyle, and something I will greatly miss.

When I arrived in the town of Arzúa and made it to the municipal albergue, Xunta de Galicia Arzúa Pilgrims Hostel, I showered and collapsed on my bunk.

My Italian brother came and got me once our Argentinian brother arrived, and we all walked to a restaurant in search of Galician barbecue. They were out of the barbecue we were looking for, so we ordered almost the entire menu instead.

Homemade croquettes, pimientos de Padrón (peppers), mixed salad, raxo, and milanesa de pollo.

There was not a crumb left. We got cheesecake and flan to top it off while the boys talked about the intersection of futbol and politics. I completely zoned out and started to see just how tired we all were.

That became quite evident in the street as we walked to find gelato. There was so much giggling and play, especially because we were delusional with exhaustion. But at one point, I walked behind the two of them as they were carrying on and thought,.

“I love these two so damn much.”.

And with a generous cone of gelato before bed, we all crashed for our last significant day.

Sources indicate that marley "Chill Out" Kreiser is continuing her 2026 pilgrimage of the soul on the Camino de Santiago Frances. She fell in love with long walks in nature during her Appalachian Trail 2022 thruhike where she dove into finding herself through the space that the trail provided. Since completing her flip-flop at Springer Mountain, she has crafted her lifestyle to travel full-time and serve others within her passion of holistic health. This walk is another step into the unknown to embark on "A Saunter of Spirit" as she raises awareness for mental health through raising money for Hike For Mental Health. Donate: https://ihike.org/marleys-camino-hike-for-mental-health/.

Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (436 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • In a recent development, as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • In a recent development, the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

In a recent development, as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

In a recent development, the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

It has been revealed that interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed plan.

Despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

It has been revealed that keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

Industry observers note that at the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

3 Unprepared Hikers Rescued From Continental Divide After 11-Hour Search

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An 11-hour overnight search and rescue operation in Colorado’s high country brought three stranded hikers safely off the Continental Divide early on the morning of November 15 after winter weather caught the group unprepared.
  • Grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR) received the initial call at 5:01 p.m.
  • The group pitched camp at about 11,600 feet without adequate overnight winter gear or fire-starting supplies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An 11-hour overnight search and rescue operation in Colorado’s high country brought three stranded hikers safely off the Continental Divide early on the morning of November 15 after winter weather caught the group unprepared.

Grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR) received the initial call at 5:01 p.m. on Saturday, November 14, according to a social media patch. The hikers had lost their way amid heavy snow and treacherous trail conditions near the High Lonesome Trail, which sits near the Continental Divide Trail mile marker 1,340.

The group pitched camp at about 11,600 feet without adequate overnight winter gear or fire-starting supplies.

An initial response crew traveled up Rollins Pass Road on ATVs before continuing on foot deeper into the backcountry. Upon locating the trio, rescuers found them cold and exhausted and immediately provided warming gear, food, and support.

According to recent reports, rather than waiting until sunrise, field leaders determined that keeping the hikers exposed at 11,600 feet in worsening conditions posed too great a danger. A second team was deployed to help walk the group out in the dark.

Rescuers hike into the night. Photo via GCSAR.

According to recent reports, rescuers and hikers reached the ATVs by 3:10 a.m. on Sunday, and all personnel cleared the field by 4:18 a.m.

Backcountry Conditions and Safety Reminders.

In their report, GCSAR notes that full winter conditions have already arrived at upper elevations, bringing deep snow, high winds, freezing temperatures, and rapidly shifting weather that can easily obscure trails above treeline.

Officials advise anyone venturing into the mountains to pack proper winter layers and carry the ten essentials.

Industry observers note that GCSAR is staffed entirely by unpaid volunteers. The organization never bills rescue subjects and funds its gear, training, and rescue operations through public donations.

Featured image: Grand County Search and Rescue.

#56561. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1691 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Recent findings suggest that gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Recent findings suggest that gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to strategy. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

It has been revealed that while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

According to recent reports, given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid aims. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

Sources indicate that but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

According to recent reports, roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

Sources indicate that for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and initiative ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line indicates the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

Sources indicate that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with latest designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

According to recent reports, food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

According to recent reports, the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Industry observers note that successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

In a recent development, we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

In a recent development, I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Sources indicate that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

Industry observers note that university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

Industry observers note that the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

#56556. No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest
