No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (384 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • In a recent development, “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is promptly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

In a recent development, “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

Sources indicate that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Sources indicate that once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Recent findings suggest that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

#56554. Breaking: Fast Paced River Fords After Flooding on the Arizona Trail

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2918 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Fast Paced River Fords After Flooding on the Arizona Trail

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this morning we got a nice early start at the room in Strawberry.
  • It has been revealed that it was nice and cold out this morning, so the hot tub felt fantastic.
  • It has been revealed that right around 9AM we were all good to go, and Woods texted me to let us know that they had just pulled up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this morning we got a nice early start at the room in Strawberry. I wanted to get all packed up and then go in the hot tub first thing! That sounded like a wonderful way to start off the day. Last night I managed to coordinate a ride out of town with a few other hikers. The same kind man, Al, who we had breakfast with the other morning offered to drive a group back to the trailhead. About 5-6 hikers are getting back on trail at a road about 38 miles further south than where we’re getting back on trail. Al’s wife actually drove all of those hikers back to trail. Then Al was going to pick up Woods, Strix, and Leaf before coming to pick up Slide and myself around 9AM. That gave us plenty of time to go in the hot tub, shower, and have a little breakfast before hitting the trail.

It has been revealed that it was nice and cold out this morning, so the hot tub felt fantastic. Slide and I soaked in there and then I took a final shower before we would be dirty hikers once more. The last couple of days off have been really nice. I needed the time to get some work done, and the trail needed some time to soak up all of the rain. I figure it we will still be dealing with the impacts of the storm for a little while, but hopefully it will be nothing in comparison to what it would have been like yesterday and the day before. After my shower I had a piece of pizza leftover from last night. Then I packed up the rest of my things and got ready to hit the road. We had talked about maybe walking down the road to the empanada place for breakfast. I absolutely love empanadas! But they didn’t open until 9AM and I didn’t want to make anyone wait for us, so we decided against it.

It has been revealed that right around 9AM we were all good to go, and Woods texted me to let us know that they had just pulled up. We loaded everything into Al’s truck and talked with everyone as we got ready to go. Strix has been dealing with some foot pain and is going to get dropped off right down the street to try and hitch into the larger town of Payson. Woods and Leaf are going to continue south on the trail just like us but will go into town sometime tomorrow from the highway crossing in 38 miles. That way they can hopefully link back up with Strix, and all continue on together from there. Slide and I are going to continue another 71 miles hopefully in the next 3 days and will head into the town of Payson in the evening. That will help to break up the next section of trail a little bit better so that we don’t have to carry as much food.

A bridge that the trail crossed over in the early evening.

The ride to the trailhead took about 30 minutes but we got there eventually. It was so incredibly nice of Al to offer us a ride. And he made sure that we all had his phone number in case anyone needed some help over the next couple of days. That was really sweet of him. Then we were back on trail once more! It feels really good to be back at it after another double zero to avoid bad weather here in Arizona. We have now taken 5 zero days in the 17 days that we have been hiking the trail, which sounds absolutely crazy. It is in stark contrast to the way that Slide and I both hiked last year on our CYTC hikes. But we have the time to do it and hiking in that weather would have been really miserable. If not seriously dangerous. There are a couple different river crossings that we will have to go through tomorrow and the next day which would have hazardous or even impassable during the heavy rain. I’m curious to see how deep they will be only a couple of days after the rain has passed.

In a recent development, almost immediately when we began hiking south, we encountered patches of mud and areas where the trail was almost completely flooded. For the first couple of miles, we managed to navigate around the wetter sections while still keeping our feet dry. But that didn’t last long. Eventually there were areas where the trail was under about 4-5 inches of water consistently, and there was no good way around it. I was pretty happy though that the trail was wetter than it was muddy. Areas like this will often get a thick mud that sticks to your shoes and cakes on heavily. Walking in mud like that for miles can make your ankles and feet incredibly sore just from the weight of the mud alone. Slipping and sliding in mud can also make my hips and knees hurt, depending on how bad the mud is. At least the trail today was much more wet than it was muddy.

In a recent development, A happy little mushroom just off the trail. All of the plants have been loving this rain.

When we were about 5 miles into the day the trail crossed over a dirt parking lot and trailhead. There were some large boulders surrounding the parking lot, so Slide and I decided to stop off there and enjoy a quick break. We’re only planning to hike around 20 miles today, so there is no need to rush. Woods and Leaf were somewhere behind us as well and it sounded nice to let everyone catch up. I was surprised how much mud and dirt was already coating my legs after only a handful of miles of hiking. The two of us hung out there for a while and then continued along. And right as we were leaving, I could see at least one of the girls approaching off in the distance. They weren’t far behind!

Caked in mud and dirt, only 5 miles after leaving town.

From there the trail continued through a forested area and we began to descend gradually. I could hear the loud roar of water off in the distance and began to wonder if we would be crossing the river that I could hear. Only a couple of miles after the trailhead where we had taken a break, we were now approaching a very large river. The trail did exactly what it always does when it requests you to cross a river. It descended all the way down until the trail disappeared and only the river laid before us. We had no choice but to cross it. The water looked deep and quite fast moving. I was not exactly eager to plunge into the freezing cold water. Slide on the other hand got right into the water and began to cross it. It’s always nice to gauge the water level on someone else before you also have to go through the water. We crossed right at the trail crossing and I could see the water rise to Slide’s upper thighs. He’s pretty tall so I knew that they water was going to be right up to the bottom of my shorts.

A river that we had to cross this morning.

I only had one trekking pole out which certainly wasn’t adequate for this crossing. The water was deep and very fast moving. With only one trekking pole I was not nearly stable enough. Plus, of course I was trying to record some videos of us crossing the water. I was glad that Slide was there on the other side. Otherwise, I would have probably had to pull my other trekking pole out to secure myself in that final stretch of the river crossing. But Slide just got back into the water and extended a hand to help me across that last little bit of river. Even though we had just stopped for a break less than an hour prior, we still decided to sit down there beside the river. I had a bunch of rocks in my shoes from crossing the river, and the girls likely weren’t far behind. They had each other so I wasn’t too worried about them. But they both are significantly shorter than Slide and me, so it seemed nice to wait around for them just in case.

Slide helping Leaf across the river.

We sat there beside the river for a while, waiting to see if the girls arrived. And just as we were thinking about packing up and continuing along, I could see one of the girls crest over the hillside on the other side of the river. So, we decided to wait just a bit longer to let them get across. The first person to appear was Leaf, and we gave her some guidance for crossing the river. It was really deep though so Slide wound up just going over to her to help. He got into the river and met her about halfway through to help bring her to the other side. Then she joined us on the shore, and we sat and talked with her for a bit. In hindsight, I’m so glad that we waited for her. Because neither Slide nor I realized that the other hiker Wood’s had actually done a road walk earlier on in the day, which meant she was no longer heading in this direction. If we had continued on, then Leaf would have been stuck going through the fast-paced river alone. Knowing that no one else was anywhere close by behind her. I’m sure she would have been alright, but I was glad that we stuck around.

The sign by the trailhead when we finally got off the dirt road and reconnected to the AZT.

Before we headed out to continue along, we told Leaf that we were hoping to go around 20 miles. Hopefully she will go the same distance, and we can all camp together later this evening. She came out here to meet up with this group and hike with everyone, and now she’s basically alone. She’ll be able to link back up with everyone tomorrow, but it would be nice for her to not have to be alone on trail tonight. From there I wasn’t sure what to expect along the trail. That river crossing was a complete surprise to me, so who knows what is up ahead of us now. We wound up climbing for a while to get up and out of the area where we crossed the river. Once we got up top of the climb, the trail was completely dry and the trail turned in a double wide dirt road. Leaf had pointed out to us that the trail actually crossed over a road that we could continue along for a little while. It would wind up reconnecting with the AZT but might give a reprieve from any possible mud.

The section of trail that we were hiking through just before dark was really beautiful.

After a mile or two we arrived at that dirt road crossing and decided to continue along the road as well. It sounded like a nice way to get a handful of miles in without too much struggle. The road was really nice and quite dry which was delightful. We walked through a bunch of different logging operations alongside the road. Trees were piled high in preparation of them being transported somewhere. We even walked by a logging camp with a bunch of recreational vehicles. I’ve heard about guys camping out and living at these types of logging operations. There were generators running and we saw a couple of guys and a dog running around. I wonder if they will have to hold off on logging for a while after all of the rain.

The sun beginning to set as we continued along the trail.

According to recent reports, the road had a lot of long hills for us to climb and descend, but eventually we began going downhill continuously for a while as we got closer to the AZT. Then we passed by another trailhead parking area and turned right to get back on the trail. The trail began descending rapidly once we reconnected to it. And we went right past a junction for some kind of mine that you can walk to right off the trail. Some hikers left comments indicating that it was a great place to hide out in bad weather. But we decided not to explore the side trail down to it today. We’ll be hiking until after dark this evening most likely and didn’t need to get sidetracked. We did stop off for another break though to put some more layers on as it was getting later. And we hoped that if we sat for a break then Leaf might catch up to us as well. Both of us really wanted her to catch up so that she wouldn’t have to camp alone tonight.

Filtering water on the AZT with my platypus QuickDraw filter.

Recent findings suggest that the area that we were hiking through had numerous trailheads scattered throughout it, so we actually wound up seeing some day hikers not long after that. The trail also followed along a creek for a handful of miles toward the end of the day. It was great to have endless access to water if we needed it. We wound up stopping off and filling up on water sometime around 5PM, just so that we wouldn’t we wouldn’t have to worry about it for the rest of the night. And not long after that, the trail crossed over yet another trailhead. This one had a trail register as well, so I decided to leave a note for Leaf. I told her how much further we planned to go for the night in case she was close behind us and was hoping to camp together as well. Then we continued on with only a handful more miles to go for the day.

Standing up from a final break before we continued on into the dark.

Sources indicate that someone built this rock fort right next to the trail. I wonder how long it’s been there for.

Sources indicate that the trail began to climb gradually after we left that trailhead. Which meant that we got wonderful views of the sunset as it began to light up the sky. It’s pretty typical for us to stop off and enjoy one final break before the sun goes down. Especially if we are hiking somewhere with great views of the sunset. This was too perfect to pass up. When we did get going again, we came across some cows that were hanging out right on the trail. I always feel bad for scaring the cows. We try to talk nicely to them when we go past, but most of the time you wind up scaring the cows either way.

The sunset this evening was incredible. It’s always my favorite time of the day!

Eventually the sun went down, and we continued on in the dark for a little while longer. The area that we were hiking through did not seem like it was going to accommodate our need for a camp spot. So, when we finally did turn a corner and see a fairly flat area we decided to take advantage of it. There were some cow pies on the ground, and it wasn’t the best spot I’d ever seen, but it would work for tonight. The two of us got our tents set up and were hopeful that any minute now we would see Leaf’s headlamp coming around the corner. But that actually never happened. She must have stopped off for the night before the sun went down. Once my tent was set up, I got comfortable and had a little bit of dinner. Then did my stretching and a little editing in my tent before calling it a night.

Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (336 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • In a recent development, the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

In a recent development, the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

According to recent reports, A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (320 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • Sources indicate that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

Sources indicate that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

It has been revealed that this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” remarked Kondrashkin.

It has been revealed that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#56543. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (614 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • It has been revealed that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

It has been revealed that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he mentioned.

In a recent development, lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

It has been revealed that lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

In a recent development, the Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line presently being attempted by a Russian team.

In a recent development, this is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

According to recent reports, kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his looks while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (698 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Foothills Trail Shakedown

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In November 2026, I took on the Foothills Trail (FHT) eastbound as my shakedown hike to test my gear, mental toughness, and physical strength.
  • Industry observers note that let’s talk about the gear I will NOT get rid of, my MVPs!
  • The nights were cold with the lowest temp at camp being 28°F one night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In November 2026, I took on the Foothills Trail (FHT) eastbound as my shakedown hike to test my gear, mental toughness, and physical strength. Stretching 77 miles through North and South Carolina, the trail challenges hikers with rugged terrain. My watch had tracked 16,132 feet of ascent and 16,584 feet of descent. My main goal was simple: focus on what gear worked and what didn’t. It turned out to be the exact wake-up call I needed before January. Some of my systems passed with flying colors, while others forced an immediate rethink.

Industry observers note that let’s talk about the gear I will NOT get rid of, my MVPs! You can find a gear list breakdown in my profile. My tent is my favorite piece of gear by a long shot. Because it’s semi-freestanding, the poles give it structure, meaning I can pitch it practically anywhere with just a few stakes. It also weighs in at just under two pounds, which is a huge advantage. My second favorite piece of gear is my new down quilt. I’m naturally cold, so having a 20°F quilt hits the spot for chilly Florida winter temps and the late-season cold snaps of southern Appalachia. It has a closed footbox to keep my feet warm and pad straps, which clip underneath my sleeping pad to keep the quilt secured and trap warm air inside.

The nights were cold with the lowest temp at camp being 28°F one night. At this time I had a 30°F quilt with an open toe box, no quilt straps, and by night two I had already decided this quilt wasn’t going to work even with my cold weather clothes. I sent many texts to my husband each night about how cold I was and even spent 45 minutes one night looking for a bail-out point for the following day which he wouldn’t learn until after my hike. Little did I know, he was one step ahead of me, as always, and had purchased a 20°F quilt for me after my first text night one. My first gear swap was complete before my shakedown trail had even really started.

Recent findings suggest that more than any single piece of gear, the Foothills Trail taught me how important it is to manage my body and timing. Taking time to stretch at the end of each day made a massive difference in keeping my muscles from locking up after hours of steep climbs and descents. I also realized that smart pacing isn’t just about hitting daily mileage goals. It’s about getting into camp with enough daylight to pitch my tent, eat dinner, and get into my warm layers before the temperature drops for the night. Walking away from those 77 miles, I feel way more confident in my gear.

Hey, I'm Cat! I've been working as a registered nurse for the last couple of years, but before that, I was a pastry chef turned correctional officer turned dental assistant. You could say I embrace change and enjoy a challenge! My husband and I lived in Colorado for six years, which is where I found my true love for the outdoors. We eloped on one of Colorado's many fourteeners with our two dogs, and since then, it has been one adventure after another. My husband, a seasoned thru-hiker, has encouraged me to embark on my own thru-hiking journey. After logging hundreds of miles in Colorado's wilderness, I completed the Foothills Trail in November 2026 as a shakedown for my upcoming trails. I'm excited to share the reality of long-distance hiking, accomplishments and challenges alike. Follow along as I trade scrubs for trail runners and take on the miles ahead!

#56538. Breaking: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1236 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • Industry observers note that what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Recent findings suggest that sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It indicated again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

Industry observers note that what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Recent findings suggest that sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Sources indicate that strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

Industry observers note that “Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

In a recent development, “Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

Industry observers note that during their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

Sources indicate that “Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

Recent findings suggest that “We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang noted. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

Industry observers note that the problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

Sources indicate that the climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

In a recent development, climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

According to recent reports, rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

Industry observers note that strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he indicates:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

It has been revealed that the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

#56535. Te Araroa: mum, please send me $32

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2163 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Te Araroa: mum, please send me $32

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After my very dark dome day, I went to bed feeling proud of myself but worried that I’d wake up feeling equally tired.
  • Notes from the trail log at the dome cafe (no longer actually a cafe).
  • We had been discussing “trail legs” for a couple of days now, wondering if maybe we were finally getting them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After my very dark dome day, I went to bed feeling proud of myself but worried that I’d wake up feeling equally tired. Much to my delight, however, I slept well and woke up feeling pretty restored. It’s amazing what a shower, some food, and a sleep will do for your body.

Notes from the trail log at the dome cafe (no longer actually a cafe).

We had been discussing “trail legs” for a couple of days now, wondering if maybe we were finally getting them. I think on this day I got my first inkling of them, we walked as a group this morning (except Charlie who we knew would catch up as she’s the fastest out of all of us) and zoomed through the first ten kilometres. It was easy gravel road and the clouds hadn’t burned off yet. I felt good despite how hard I’d found the day before.

In a recent development, sinèad, Annabel and I stopped for a snack break before the final hill portion of the day. The sun had started to burn off the clouds at this point, and it was starting to get hot. But we knew we only had about 15km into Puhoi (where we’d find food and maybe even a beer), and a campsite in 10km where we could replenish our water. So we pushed on.

This section of the day was a slog, not because the terrain was hard (it was just a gravel road) but because the sun was so hot. Saying we were sweaty would be an understatement, but there was nowhere to stop to cool off because the whole track was exposed. So we pushed on.

At some point Charlie did catch us and we all continued our climb up the gravel hill. This was the moment that I really decided that my merino hoodie was going to have to go. Luckily I have Fraser at home with access to my lighter-weight synthetic sun hoodies so I got him to send one to my friend in Auckland. Feels nice to not have to spend money unnecessarily.

According to recent reports, eventually, like finding an oasis in a desert, we spotted a little side track that led to a grassy, shaded area. I made a beeline for it and dropped all my stuff. It was approaching noon and I decided it was lunch time so took off my sun hoodie and pulled out my remaining trail pizza ingredients. This break was such a relief!

After drinking about half a litre of water and eating my two wraps (this time with added chilli flavoured corn nuts for crunch), I felt fortified enough to keep walking in the sun.

It has been revealed that the rest of the afternoon passed in a sweaty blur and soon we found ourselves descending a strange path between two paddocks toward the Remiger road campsite at km 533. At this point I had pretty much run out of water so I powered ahead, focused on the water tank I knew was at the camp. It was a beautiful camp with a nice shelter, and after our 20 very hot kilometres it was a really great place for a break.

Recent findings suggest that we had decided the night before that we’d try to make it into Puhoi and the call of the pub was strong enough to keep us from pitching tents at Remiger road. After a decent, shoe off, stretch out kind of break we were ready to conquer the final 4.5km of road walking.

According to recent reports, with eternal hope in our hearts, we gave hitching a go, but people only sped up when they saw us. Thanks, Auckland.

Industry observers note that once we realized that hitching wasn’t going to happen, we began our road walk to Puhoi. It went surprisingly rapidly and soon Charlie was dancing and waving her poles out front of the Puhoi tea rooms.

Annabel, Charlie, me and Sinèad at the tea rooms after checking in. Photo courtesy of Sinèad.

Industry observers note that the tea rooms were our home for the night, for $10 you get a very non-private shower (but there’s hot water so I’m not complaining), wifi, charging, and a tent site. The owner also does a special offer for TA hikers where he re-opens the cafe just for us and will make you anything off the menu or a burger. This seemed much nicer than walking a further 500m to the pub and was probably also cheaper, so we all agreed to stay in for the night.

It has been revealed that we also met up with Moritz who had taken a zero at the tea rooms. He was full of energy and went to the shop to buy us snacks and used his flip fuel to top up our gas canisters. Before I left for Te Araroa I told Fraser I was sure I’d meet someone who would be able to do that, and once again: the trail provides.

I went to bed full and happy, and with the knowledge that because of tides, we’d have a very slow morning and then a chill 8km kayak down the Puhoi river the next day.

With our kayaks booked at 1pm, we had a slow morning. I had time to blog, charge all my electronics, dry my tent and order my blasphemous breakfast (see blog post about food for more). It was a luxurious morning and included coffee!!

At about 11:30am we headed toward the pub and general store where I did a small resupply and got some lunch and another coffee. I was not messing around with coffee anymore, not after how I felt on the dome day.

It has been revealed that at 1pm, we made our way to the kayak place, got our briefing, and dropped off our packs. The awa (river) is the official TA trail, which is pretty cool! It requires an outgoing tide, so the moon and ocean and river decide what time your day starts. It felt sort of lovely to know that we didn’t have a choice of when we started. The awa has long served as a highway for waka (boats) and its name translates to “slow water”.

Industry observers note that the awa is aptly named, and the kayak down it was so peaceful. I spent a lot of time just being carried by the current and paddling intermittently only to steer. Though the highway now runs over and beside the awa, it’s still a lovely space. As I paddled down, I watched the water turn from a murky brown river to clear, salinated ocean water.

A penguin floated past and I desperately tried to point it out for the people behind me. As I approached the end of the river, I spotted rays. It was magical.

Recent findings suggest that once off the kayaks, everyone agreed that it would be rude not to swim. So we got in the now ocean water. It was refreshing, and so warm compared to the water I’m used to swimming in in Wellington. The ground, however, was a whole strange experience. I spent most of the swim trying to keep my feet from touching the gooey mud on the bottom and Annabel and I screamed as our feet sank in.

It was a nice, silly afternoon.

According to recent reports, soon we were all back in our dry clothes, socks and dry-ish shoes. We stated bye to Anica who was nursing an Achilles injury, which was sad.

Industry observers note that there wasn’t much left in the day and we’d have to wait for a tidal section on the other side of a small hill. We set off anyway, and got our legs back into the habit of walking after our lazy morning and kayak.

On top of the hill between the end of the Puhoi and Waiwera.

Sources indicate that by the time we reached Waiwera (which translates to hot water because of the hot springs in the area) Charlie and I were not feeling keen to wait for the tides. My beach-blisters were hurting and making me feel like I was limping, and Charlie was just generally not feeling well. We decided to split up, and she and I took a bus into Ōrewa to check us all into the campground while the other two waited for the tides.

Charlie on the bus – she has a very similar shot of me.

Industry observers note that the Ōrewa holiday park was by far the worst place we’ve stayed. The “tent sites” were actually just hard-packed ground with a ton of tree roots. But the staff were really nice and I decided I’d ask at the office how much it would cost to upgrade to a cabin (it ended up being $1.25 extra each). I’m so glad I did!! There were some strange characters at the park and one guy told us that his laundry had been stolen the night before, so it felt nice to have a lock on the door.

According to recent reports, our little cabin was soon full of tents drying out, and dry bags jammed into every corner. We pondered whether we could fit Moritz in on the floor but luckily another hiker, Tim, had booked the cabin beside ours so he got a real bed.

What else would thru-hikers do at night.

It has been revealed that I was happy to leave Ōrewa, and knew we were heading for a massive supermarket and shopping mall. The walk this morning was easy and quick into Silverdale, where we all split up to run our respective errands. I spent way too much money buying blister plasters and restocking my supplements at chemist warehouse, but offset that by NOT buying a pastry at the coffee shop.

Sources indicate that caffeinated and ready to go, we packed up our new things and started the walk to Stillwater. This was all road and started relatively pleasantly with wide sidewalks and grassy shoulders. But eventually we got on the final stretch of road to Stillwater and it became the worst road we had encountered on the whole trail so far. Significant trucks blasted past us and we scrambled to not fall into the steep ditches. When we finally came to a spot where someone could pick us up, Annabel, Sinèad and I decide to try to hitch.

Charlie, being ever the bravest of us, continued along the road and said the road did eventually get better.

According to recent reports, A lovely couple picked us up and started telling us about a cabin we could stay in along the Ōkura walkway. This led to them calling their daughter who mentioned that the cabin was SO FAR into the walk, like thirty minutes. We all laughed out loud at that and then she asked her mum to send her $32. Walking the bulk of that scary road was made worth it by that one phone call.

Sources indicate that the couple dropped us off at the end of the road, and we ate our lunch at a little park before joining the Ōkura walkway. We got lucky with tides and were able to skirt the edges of the coast for this walk and very promptly found ourselves at Dacre Cottage. This was a gorgeous campsite with a shelter, toilets, water and some pretty nice, flat spaces to pitch tents. We were there early but the next kilometre or so involved a tidal crossing and it wasn’t low tide until 8pm. We would have to wait until the morning and cross at low tide.

In a recent development, once again the TA fearmongering began. We had received videos from Sven who crossed a day or two before us showing everyone in their undies with the water up to their chests. I decided it would be fun even if it was meant to rain tomorrow. And besides, we all had indoor beds booked tomorrow night so it didn’t matter if all our stuff got soaked, right?

#56534. Breaking: A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1958 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • The two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.
  • Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a newly introduced route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

The two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a newly introduced route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential upcoming line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Industry observers note that beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

It has been revealed that they climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

They called their fresh line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Industry observers note that later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

In a recent development, skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

In a recent development, one thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

Can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

The two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Recent findings suggest that another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

In a recent development, here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

Currently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

Recent findings suggest that how many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

In a recent development, during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

We had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive big walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Industry observers note that yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

It has been revealed that patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

Recent findings suggest that the granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

You climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

Sources indicate that there were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

From there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

At the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

According to recent reports, all belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

Recent findings suggest that as in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

According to recent reports, how much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

Industry observers note that the most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a latest route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

Your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

Industry observers note that most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other major-wall areas?

In a recent development, we were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

#56531. Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (796 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • According to recent reports, with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

According to recent reports, with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

It has been revealed that A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

The skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

Sources indicate that the accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

Other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police mentioned the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident shows that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

The accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

Recent findings suggest that the avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

Industry observers note that the second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Sources indicate that fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the major powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them plan to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Sources indicate that snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) shows low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

According to recent reports, the avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps reveals remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.
