#56529. Industry News: From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3986 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass.
  • Probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm!
  • Recent findings suggest that fortunately, that did the trick.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  48,865 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  22:07.

Sources indicate that the night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass. In addition to the extra mileage, I also figured it would be warmer at that lower elevation. The camping spot I selected, looking out at a huge golden, grassy meadow, was lovely.

Probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm! It was already chilly when I went to sleep, and as the night went on it just got colder and colder. I gradually added items to my sleeping bag — sleeping bag liner, long pants, long shirt, puffy hat, gloves — until I used up the entirety of my anti-cold arsenal.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, that did the trick. But had it been just a little colder, I would have been overwhelmed. It created a cognitive conflict during my pee errands in the night. My temperature sensors urged me to return to the tent as promptly as possible. My spiritual-aesthetic soul urged me to spend just a little more time under the glorious blanket of moon and stars.

Industry observers note that towards morning, I had a bizarre dream. It this alternate reality, I was having a hot affair with a woman. Actually, it was a cold affair. Why? Because she was really an alien, part of an extraterrestrial race that was thinking of settling on earth, but who didn’t like our climate. It was too hot for them. Having superior technology, however, they were able to manipulate Earth climate and make it much colder to their liking. So, I was freezing cold, despite having this torrid affair.

Another capability of the alien was that she could make you mostly forget what you had done the night before. So, I kind of knew I was having the affair, but also wasn’t completely sure that I was. The hilarious part was that the alien in the dream was my wife’s friend DG from middle school! When I told Lee about the dream, I had to swear that I had never, ever contemplated having an affair with DG!

Did this moonlight view up through the tent inspire my strange dream?

When it began to get light, I gave myself a little bit of a break because it had been so cold. My last trip outside the tent in the early dawn I looked out on that golden meadow and saw that it was all white, coated with icy rime.

By the time I took this picture, the rime was already melting, but some is still visible.

I also retrieved my bear cannister; it too had a layer of ice on the top cover.

In close-up, the ice on the bear cannister is very visible.

According to recent reports, by this I knew it had gone below freezing during the night. So, I allowed myself some extra minutes of warmth in the sleeping bag while I waited for the sun to rise above the lip of the mountains.

I finally got up at 6:30. When the sun came up the temperature rose quickly, but the problem then was that the ice on my tent fly became moisture. Also, the floor was pitched on a sort of pine needle-covered mud. This was very comfortable, but it ended up sticking to my ground sheet. It took some time and effort to get everything dry and clean.

After all the morning errands, I did not get on the road until – wait for it – ten a.m.! On a short day, that might not have mattered, but I was planning another 17+ miles for this day. The good news was, that I was camped in the Lyell Valley, and the mostly flat trail followed the Lyell Fork river for almost nine miles, all the way to Tuolumne Meadows.

Sometimes the river and trail were close like this, sometimes farther apart.

With this cruisy route (and my late departure) I turned on the jets as I headed out. With my unfortunate record of falling on easy trails, I was also trying to be careful.

Hard to get lost on this trail!

Sources indicate that A good portion of the trail, especially in the meadows, was indented into the earth. My feet were below the ground level in a narrow track. In this configuration, I find that hiking poles are more hazard than help. So, for most of the first nine miles, I was carrying my poles rather than using them.

The statistics tell the tale. Over those nine miles, I was only over 20 minutes (3 mph) twice. My best mile I did in 17:49. That is no record speed, but I don’t think I was even close to that pace anywhere else on the trail.

Industry observers note that the scenery was interesting, but not spectacular. The main thing, with this wide-open valley, was that I could measure my progress visually. I could see an unusual-shaped mountain lining the valley up ahead; then after a time it was closer; then I was opposite to it; and then it was starting to fall behind me. In a slower progression, I could see the distant mountains at the foot of the valley ahead (where the river changes direction). At first, they were far distant, then middle distant, and eventually they were quite close.

The wide glacial valley, filled with meadows, and the mountains at the far end that grew larger as I got closer.

It has been revealed that at faster than 3 mph, I was in Tuolumne Meadows in under three hours. As I got closer it was apparent there was a tourist center nearby. Suddenly many more persons were on the trail and most of them were geared out for just a day of hiking or fishing.

Industry observers note that the design of Tuolumne was a little weird, with a “downtown” road (Tioga Road) on the north side of the river and a hiking trail parallel on the south side. I generally don’t love road-walking. However, because the Wilderness Center (for permits) was in the middle of downtown, and because I wanted a permit to climb Half Dome the next day, I intended to go via the road.

NPS map of Tuolumne Meadows (in the lower right, I should have turned onto the “National Scenic Trail” but instead stayed on the John Muir Trail).

It has been revealed that I missed the turn. Maybe my feet just wanted to stay in the woods? As I realized my error, I ran into a really nice couple who were staying at the fancy lodge nearby. They had a map, and they confirmed, “Yeah, you just have to go back to that last turn and then turn to go across the river, instead of going straight.”.

It has been revealed that I had a sudden aversion to that blueprint, particularly because of the miles I wanted to hike that day. The woman must have seen my expression, because she said, “My husband is just like you; he hates to backtrack!”.

It was true. So, I stated, “Maybe I’ll go to the Visitor Center instead, and they can help me there.”  I continued on.

Recent findings suggest that now I was surrounded by roads and parking lots. As I passed one lot, I saw a uniformed ranger manning the booth and I walked up to him. When I explained what I wanted, he said, “First of all, to get a permit, you have to go to the Wilderness Center. Second, they will not give you a permit to climb Half Dome. The only way to get a Half Dome permit is to get a whole different multi-day permit that includes climbing Half Dome within it.”.

Now that had not been my understanding, but he seemed very confident. At this point I was even further away from the Wilderness Center and even less inclined to backtrack. I could see my Half Dome ambitions evaporating. I figured I could still go to the Visitor Center and give it one last try.

In a recent development, en route I saw that I would pass the market that hosted the famous Tuolumne Grill, and I realized that it was just about lunchtime. I left my pack outside and went in to order. It seemed a simple layout with some picnic tables outside to eat what you ordered. I got a regular hamburger that came with orange juice and some wedge potatoes. The juice tasted delicious on this now-hot day, and the wedges, slathered with ketchup, were good too. But the hamburger? It was an ordinary sort of dry hockey puck, not terrible, but not special at all. I concluded the Grill was famous because of where it was, and not for what it served.

Industry observers note that as I ate it all, I took my phone off of Airplane Mode and called my wife, Lee. (I always hike with it in Airplane Mode to preserve my battery charge.)  When I told her the likely newly introduced proposal, without Half Dome, she sounded excited that I was almost done. I was looking forward to seeing her soon as well.

The Visitor Center was a mile-long road walk from there. I had two animal encounters (of a sort) along the way.

In a recent development, first, I saw wild turkeys! How funny to spend all that time in the wilderness without seeing any (though I did see grouse). Then in congested Tuolumne I saw them. I even got some pictures.

If not for the legs, the turkey blended in….

Second, as I was walking, a car slowed way down opposite me and the driver shouted out his window, “A bear just walked across the road up ahead less than five minutes ago!”.

I shouted back, “Good! I hope I see him, because I am getting really hungry!”.

According to recent reports, whether he was pulling my leg, or he really saw the bear, I did not see any bear. I was definitely looking out for it though.

Industry observers note that after pine forest and silence, it was disconcerting to walk on asphalt with diesel engines roaring past me. I was glad it was only a mile. On arrival, I went up to the very nice woman in front of the Visitor Center and asked about permits. No surprise, she directed me to the Wilderness Center. I concluded the fates did not intend me to climb Half Dome.

Then I asked about getting out of Yosemite when I reached Happy Isles. She explained about the free shuttle within the park that could get me to Curry Village from Happy Isles if I didn’t want to walk there. From Curry Village, the YARTS (Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System) could transport me for a fee. The end of their line was Merced, about three hours away. I figured I could take a train or bus from Merced, or maybe Gabriel could come from Santa Rosa and pick me up there.

It has been revealed that this lady pointed to the YARTS timetable on their bulletin board and suggested I take a picture of it. I replied, “That’s a great idea! You’re a lot smarter than I am to think of it!”.

She also gave me a paper map of the Yosemite Valley to include Happy Isles and Curry Village, saying, “I know you hikers don’t like to add weight, but I think you might find this useful.”.

I told her I was sure I would and stashed it away.

Recent findings suggest that with that, I aimed for the trail, which passed a ways behind the Visitor Center. It was a relief to be walking on pine needles again!

It is funny how rapidly the crowds taper off as you get even a short distance away from the tourist centers.

The other substantial change was in elevation profile. In the morning, the trail had ranged from flat to slightly downhill. Now I would face climbing up past Cathedral Lakes to Cathedral Pass. This was the last pass on the John Muir Trail. It was about 9,700 feet which was a lot lower than the passes in the south, but still more than 1,000 feet above Tuolumne Meadows.

In a recent development, perhaps it was my energy expenditure in the morning, but now I was puffing and panting as I ascended. “Where is my juice?” I asked myself. “This is as bad as climbing Cottonwood Pass on the first day of the JMT!”.

I was breathing hard, but enjoying the enormous granite rock.

The inspiration was the views. There was more than one rocky shape that could qualify as a “cathedral.”  Imagine Notre Dame. Imagine that the roof is one thousand feet high, the spires soar over 1,500 feet, and the nave stretch two miles. Then imagine a landscape dotted with two or three of these behemoths. It was magical.

About the time my legs finally got warmed up, I came across a couple that were on the first day of their John Muir Trail hike. The reversal I had imagined, when encountering near-finishers at the start of my own hike, was coming true. In chatting, he warned me, “Oh, there’s no water except at Upper Cathedral.”.

I appreciated that intel and was on the lookout for a spot near Upper Cathedral Creek. As I ascended, coming above the tree line, I was surprised not to find it. Then, as I passed a quarter mile from Upper Cathedral Lake, I saw some people emerge on a trail from the lake onto the main trail. Suddenly it dawned on me that there was no creek. He meant the lake!

It was late afternoon and I wanted to press on and find a campsite. But if this was really “last water” it would be foolish not to take the detour for it.

The lake seemed to have mostly marshy and muddy access points. These would entail wet feet and dirty water to filter. However, I saw a rocky promontory jutting into the lake where a bunch of guys were hanging out. I headed there to refill my water.

In a recent development, I began chatting with them and learned they were from Kansas City. I asked them whether they lived in Kansas or Missouri and they stated that only someone who knows Kansas City would ask that question. I explained that I had a cousin who lived in K.C. and they told me they lived on the Kansas side.

Overall, they were nice enough, but the banter occasionally felt a little mocking. For example, they asked me, “Did you go up Whitney?”   I replied that I had, but that I had been fighting a respiratory infection, making it very difficult.

They responded, “Oh, that just adds to your story about climbing Mount Whitney. Like, ‘everybody else just climbed it, but I climbed it with a respiratory infection, coughing every step of the way!’”.

They were actually not wrong, but the tone felt a little snarky.

In a recent development, after I filled both my water bottles and my Katadyn BeFree to have maximum water available, I headed back toward the trail. One of the guys, maybe the leader, followed me a short distance and called me over. He was asking me about the trail, and it turned out he had done the trail himself a few years before. It seemed a little odd, but I took him as just wanting to reminisce a bit about his own experience.

In a recent development, in a quarter mile I was back at the junction with the JMT. The beauty of the scenery around Cathedral Lakes is so inspiring, I wanted to take some more pictures. John Muir himself noted, on summiting Cathedral Peak, “This I may say is the first time I have been at church in California, led here at last, every door graciously opened for the poor lonely worshiper.”  (Quoted from My First Summer in the Sierra, Chapter 10, entry for September 7, 1869.).

In a recent development, so, this “lonely worshiper” reached for his smart phone to capture the majestic giants and discovered… nothing. Nothing at all, a black screen. Now my eyesight is not great without glasses, but I had thought my phone demonstrated 65% of charge when last I checked.

Recent findings suggest that in case it had just shut off for some reason, I tried to restart it, but still nothing. I was crestfallen, thinking, “Oh no! My phone died here on the trail with barely one day left on my hike!!!”.

I could not fathom how it happened. I had not dropped it that I could recall. Deeply disappointed, I began having paranoid thoughts. “If I had charge, and now suddenly I don’t, could that guy who followed me, to talk to me, have had some technology that fried my phone? Like some super magnet or something?”.

It seemed wildly implausible, but the coincidence – that it happened right after our exchange – seemed strange.

It has been revealed that then I calmed down somewhat. I reminded myself of what was truly important,  “This trip is about the experience itself. It is not ultimately about telling the story or capturing the pictures, it is about your lived experience.”.

Seen through that prism my loss was minor and I settled down. My wife and I always try to distinguish “disappointments” from “tragedies,” and this was clearly the former.

With the light turning to a mellow glow in the sky, I continued hiking. Cathedral Pass was not much further. It was unusual, in that the trail reached the pass, but did not descend from there down the other side. Instead, it continued on, ascending further up the ridge of one of the mountainsides bordering the pass.

Recent findings suggest that now my lack of a phone was frustrating because I had lost my navigation device. I was not sure how far I should ideally go before selecting a camp, remembering that I wanted to make miles to ensure I could finish on the following day.

Recent findings suggest that the mountains answered that question for me. As I continued higher, I came to a turn on the outstretched flank of the range. Extending from the trail was a large flat spot, with visibility in all directions. The ground was ideal for pitching a tent. The views were magical in the waning light. I thought, “I can go further, and shorten my day tomorrow. Or I can camp tonight in the most beautiful spot in the Sierras.”  That decision was an easy one.

Recent findings suggest that in Tuolumne I heard we were in for another icy night, and I was now at a higher elevation than I had been the night before. So, I was expecting cold. In fact, as the sun dropped behind the peaks, I could feel the chill almost immediately.

It has been revealed that I started to pitch my tent, and maybe I was in too much of a hurry? I love my Big Agnes TigerWall, but on this night, as I tried to get a pole into the slot, the pole snapped. After the dead phone, this might have been a devastating blow. But in this stunning location, on the last night I needed a tent, it did not phase me. Besides, I had been carrying a seemingly useless stupid little tube for miles and miles, wondering why I bothered, and now I had my answer. I slid the tube over the broken spot, taped it in place with surgical tape (though that might have been unnecessary), and reseated the pole in the slot. Good as new? Maybe not, but close enough.

Having pitched my tent, I just basked in the beauty of the location for a few minutes. Then I soaked my food and found a spot for a cat hole and dug what was likely to be my last cat hole on the trail. The cold soak did not take long, but the result was the opposite of the previous night’s dinner. That food had not rehydrated fully but was wonderfully seasoned and tasted delicious. This night the mashed potatoes and chicken hydrated easily, but they were totally bland. They didn’t taste bad really, they just didn’t taste like anything at all!

Of course, mindful as always that this is fuel first and flavor second, I wolfed it all down.

With no phone, I was communicating with my family by Garmin. That was so onerous, typing out everything, one letter at a time. (On the trail I learned of an app that makes this easier, but I didn’t have either the app or a working phone.)  Gabriel seemed amenable to picking me up in Merced, and so I realized I needed to make big speed the next day to get to Happy Isles. The 4:50 p.m. YARTS departure to Merced arrived by 8:30 p.m. Even that would mean getting back to Santa Rosa by midnight, after all. Our back and forth about this on the Garmin was practically in code, but I thought the plan was set.

According to recent reports, wrapping up my chores in deep twilight, I stored everything in my bear cannister and – why not? — I hooked my phone to the charger.

Before going to sleep, I decided to just take a peek at the phone. What?? Yes! Yes!! My phone was charging!!!

According to recent reports, I was elated and still baffled as to how it happened. I could not be sure. The best explanation I came up with was this:  First, without my glasses I had misread the charge level on the phone. It did not have 65%, it must have had much less. Second, after speaking with my wife from the restaurant at lunch, I must not have turned Airplane Mode back on, so that the phone drained far more rapidly in the afternoon than it did in the morning. That is my best guess. Operator error.

The most beautiful campsite — taken under the stars, after my phone revived.

Snuggled in my tent, I got gussied up, wearing all of my clothing in preparation for a second icy cold night.

My tent in the moonlight of the last night — repaired and welcoming (except for the mess inside!).

In a recent development, it boggled my mind to think that – most probably – I was wrapped in my sleeping bag for the last time this year. The excitement of (hopefully) completing the trail the next day would normally have kept me wide awake. But no. I was just too tired and slept right away.

  • His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment.
  • His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

In a recent development, today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police confirmed that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (623 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the fresh route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).
  • In a recent development, expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited.
  • According to recent reports, siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the fresh route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

In a recent development, expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

According to recent reports, siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

The three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

In a recent development, sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

Industry observers note that along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist says the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

The climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

Industry observers note that that night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast declared a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

It has been revealed that the last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

It has been revealed that the sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

#56519. Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (465 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (465 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • Industry observers note that initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

Industry observers note that initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

It took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

At first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

Sources indicate that A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

Industry observers note that yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

According to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

It has been revealed that as Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold new routes here.

According to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

#56510. Latest Update: How to Shoot a Shotgun (and Hit Every Bird) Like Your Granddaddy Did

Latest Update: How to Shoot a Shotgun (and Hit Every Bird) Like Your Granddaddy Did

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Don Zutz, 43, has hunted and fished all his life and has won or scored high in many skeet and trap tournaments.
  • In a recent development, harry couldn’t understand it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Don Zutz, 43, has hunted and fished all his life and has won or scored high in many skeet and trap tournaments. He was the 1964 Wisconsin skeet co-champion in 12 gauge with 100 straight and shot 150 straight in the shootoff. This story was originally published in the November 1976 glitch of Outdoor Life.

In a recent development, harry couldn’t understand it. He was a lifelong duck hunter and had never had any trouble hitting his share of waterfowl. His season birds-to-shells-fired average was quite impressive. That very morning, in fact, I had watched him drop a lone honker and a pair of passing mallards with only four shots. And on previous occasions when he forsook his beloved blinds for pheasant hunting, he had more than held his own.

It has been revealed that but Harry’s bubble burst when I suggested that we switch to open-bored guns and visit a few grouse covers after our early-morning duck hunt. It was a new world for him. Three roaring flushes from grouse netted him only half a dozen empty shells to reload. Then he missed a spiraling woodcock. Harry was beside himself with frustration and embarrassment.

“How can I be deadly at dawn and then turn into a flub by midday?” he growled.

Sources indicate that at first I didn’t pay attention. Anyone can have a bad day on grouse. When he continued to growl about his troubles over a hot cup of coffee, however, the reason for his bad showing became obvious.

“I guess those fantails are just too fast and tricky for me,” he mused. “When ducks and geese come over, I’ve got plenty of time to measure off my lead, but I simply can’t get ahead of these crazy grouse and swing with them—especially when they’re twisting through the brush!”.

Sources indicate that anyone who is conversant with the various wing-gunning methods immediately realizes that Harry had been using the wrong technique in the thickets. Instead of building his lead with a fast swing, he had used the deliberate, precise method of leading that he had perfected during all those years of dedicated duck hunting. And because it had also worked well on pheasants in the open, Harry had never questioned his method. For him, a carefully held sustained lead was the way to go. It was his one and only wingshooting technique.

It has been revealed that but deliberate shotgun pointing doesn’t work on fast-breaking game in thick cover. The hunter simply cannot measure off a precise lead and maintain it on a grouse that is threading its way through branches. Harry found out that a versatile wingshot selectively employs different methods of leading flying targets, depending on what he is shooting.

There are four basic techniques for slapping a lead on speeding birds, clay or feathered: 1) the sustained lead, otherwise known as the maintained lead; 2) the swing-through method, alias the fast swing; 3) the pull-ahead system; and 4) the snap shot (see sketches).

The one Harry had been perfecting in duck blinds, lo those many seasons, was the sustained lead. This is the method called “maintained lead” by the late, great D. Lee Braun, an outstanding Remington skeet and trap pro, in his popular book “Skeet Shooting with D. Lee Braun.”.

It has been revealed that the shooter visualizes the amount of lead he will need for a given target flying at a given speed and then brings his gun up ahead of the target by that approximate distance. Swinging at about the target’s speed, he then adjusts for the exact lead and continues swinging on the bird’s apparent line of flight until he is satisfied that the alignment and forward allowance are perfectly correct. The trigger is pulled while the gun maintains the established lead and swing speed. If the shooter judges his lead correctly, and if he maintains his lead and swing speed by following through properly, he should center his birds.

Sources indicate that the sustained lead, like all the others, is subject to human error. The shooter who gets lazy during his swing will slow down unwittingly and shoot behind. Ditto for the gunner who tries being too precise, because any tendency to aim a scattergun like a rifle results in tightening up, which also slows the swing. The most common failing, however, is stopping the swing at trigger time, thus cancelling out the forward allowance.

It has been revealed that many hunters miss with the sustained-lead method because they don’t measure off enough lead. In other words, they overestimate shot-string speed. Even at skeet’s meager 20-yard range, the low-house target at Station 3 and the high-house clay at Station 5 (right-angle-birds) require a full four-foot lead if you use this method. Passing ducks doing 70 feet per second at 40 yards require an 8½-foot lead, even with a high-velocity load of 4’s doing 1,330 feet per second at the muzzle. Stretch that range to 60 yards, and the lead increases to 14 feet! In other words, you might visualize a rowboat between the duck and your shotgun’s muzzle while also keeping the swing crisp and smooth at the duck’s speed!

Recent findings suggest that A sustained lead is best employed in the open on targets flying a steady course. It is natural when hunting doves, ducks, and geese, firing at crossing skeet clays, and for certain pheasant-hunting situations.

Sources indicate that but the sustained lead can’t be used effectively in the brush on fast-flushing birds. There isn’t enough time, and the game seldom flies a steady course. I pointed this out to Harry.

“Guess I’ll have to start snap shooting, if I want some grouse,” he remarked.

I didn’t like that idea either, and tried to dissuade him. Snap shooting is the least-scientific and least-consistent shotgun technique. It consists of nothing more than picking a spot ahead of the moving target, pointing the muzzle at that spot, and firing. There is no swing; there is no attempt to coordinate with the target’s speed; there is no follow-through. The gun is merely snapped, or poked, and it is virtually stationary, when the shot charge is triggered. If the shooter “guesstimates” right, he scores. Otherwise it’s a miss. And misses always outnumber the hits.

Sources indicate that this is not to say that snap shooting doesn’t play a role in modern wingshooting. When a hunter is caught completely off guard and can’t recover in time to make a coordinated swing, his only chance lies in a snap shot.

Sources indicate that in my opinion, about the only time snap shooting is really best is when you are trying for cottontails in the brambles. Those bounding, zigzagging, change-of-pace artists seldom allow you to take a smooth swing, and a hunter must resort to the “poke-and-hope” method. (For very different opinions on snap shooting, see Robert W. Woodruff on quail in “Five Topflight Gunners Tell How” in the October 1976 glitch of this magazine, and Peter Miller on woodcock on page 72 of this issue.).

It has been revealed that many skeet and trap shooters use a variation of snap shooting that they call spot shooting. This specialized technique has arisen because most clay-target shooters already have their guns mounted and pointed at a specific spot when the claybird appears. They do not have to bring their guns to their shoulders from a low, field-carry position. In trap, the first bird of doubles is often spot shot, because the shooters know exactly where it will be. Many skeetmen “spot” the high-house bird at Station 1 and the low-house disc at Station 7. But since a hunter doesn’t walk around with a mounted gun, and since he doesn’t know when or where the birds will appear or how they will fly, spot shooting has little application afield.

“I’d sooner see you try the swing-through method,” I told Harry. “It’s more dependable and consistent, and once you get the timing right, it can be lightning quick. In fact, some people call it the fast swing instead of the swing-through.”.

“Well, right now I’ll try anything,” Harry muttered, spinning the cap back onto his thermos.

Recent findings suggest that I explained that the shooter starts his gun behind the target. He then swings aggressively, catches up with the bird, and strokes right through it with a muzzle speed faster than the target’s flight. The mental command to fire is given just as the muzzle passes the moving mark, and the gun continues its accelerating swing along the target’s line of flight.

Sources indicate that theoretically, the correct lead is built up by the rapidly swinging gun while the shooter’s muscles respond to the mental command to fire and while the trigger yields, the firing pin falls, the primer ignites, the powder burns, and the shot charge clears the barrel. The faster the swing, the longer the lead will be. The muzzle moves ahead of the target during the shooter’s physical responses and the gun’s lock and combustion time.

Sources indicate that the swing-through system can be applied to more different hunting, skeet, and trap situations than any other method. I’ve even come to favor it over sustained lead for distant birds, because the accelerating, “heave-ho” swing needed to generate leads of eight to 15 feet after coming from behind develops a gun momentum which, in turn, insures a good, positive follow-through.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, however, some people can’t handle the true swing-through method. They don’t feel comfortable starting behind the bird. They are doubtful about swinging with gusto, and lack the timing needed to coordinate trigger pull with swinging muzzle.

According to recent reports, harry was one of them. After years of starting his gun ahead of ducks and geese and taking a deliberate, measured lead, he didn’t like swinging from behind and firing with no visually apparent lead.

But there was still hope. The following weekend I had him try a variation called the pull-ahead method. With this technique the hunter starts by bringing his gun up right on the bird. Then he builds up gun momentum by pulling ahead for a very short distance. Once he has gun alignment and momentum, the shooter moves the muzzle ahead of the bird. When the right amount of daylight appears between muzzle and bird, the trigger is pulled while the swing continues to accelerate. The amount of visual lead is supplemented by the time that elapses during the shooter’s body responses, the function of the gun, and the shot bore travel.

According to recent reports, the pull-ahead method does require good timing. There is only one point during the accelerating swing when the muzzle is in correct juxtaposition to the target. In general, though, the average person masters the pull-ahead faster than he does the swifter movement required by the true swing-through.

Recent findings suggest that although the pull-ahead method hasn’t received much publicity, I’m certain many shotgunners use it unwittingly while thinking that they are employing the true swing-through. Thousands of skeet and trap shooters align directly on their clays first and then generate leads merely by swinging crisply ahead. The business portion of their swings never starts behind the targets, and yet many of them think they are swinging through. There’s nothing wrong with that, of course, but I believe a shooter should try to understand exactly what he is doing, not what he thinks he’s doing!

Industry observers note that in the field, pull-ahead shooting works nicely with incoming birds and close-range shots at upland birds. It also works well with rabbits when the cover is fairly open. This method is faster than sustained lead, less complex than the swing-through, and more dependable than snap shooting.

Read Next: How to Miss Fewer Birds.

Sources indicate that harry picked it up easily. He felt comfortable coming up with the muzzle on the bird rather than behind it, and he liked seeing daylight between barrel and bird. But he knew better than to look for a precise, measured lead. He still uses the sustained lead for ducks because there is more time and open sky. In the brush, he found, it is simply a matter of getting on target, swinging ahead briskly, and letting go with a positive follow-through.

Recent findings suggest that this doesn’t mean pulling ahead can be used for all kinds of shooting. I seriously doubt that its abbreviated swing, starting on the bird, can develop enough gun momentum to generate the really long leads needed for distant crossing shots at waterfowl.

Industry observers note that to be a versatile wingshot, the scattergunner must have more than a single swing/lead system in his repertoire. He should learn the strengths and weaknesses of all four basic techniques, practice them with claybirds until the movements are automatic, and then apply the appropriate method as field conditions and individual shots dictate. There is no other way to become a successful all-around performer with the bird gun.

#56507. The 10 Best Walleye Fishing Tips for Early Ice

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1377 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

The 10 Best Walleye Fishing Tips for Early Ice

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s hard to believe in late December we are still talking early ice, but in the Midwest unseasonable warmer temperatures have kept water open.
  • In a recent development, safety is an crucial consideration for any sort of fishing, especially early ice.
  • Sources indicate that in most cases, ice anglers like to be mobile, drilling holes in the ice until they find fish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s hard to believe in late December we are still talking early ice, but in the Midwest unseasonable warmer temperatures have kept water open. Northern Minnesota and North Dakota, however, are experiencing some excellent early ice walleye fishing and the remainder of the Midwest shouldn’t be too far behind, so get those batteries charged and hooks sharpened because ice fishing season is coming. Here are 10 tips that will help you land more walleyes as lakes begin to freeze.

In a recent development, safety is an crucial consideration for any sort of fishing, especially early ice. Never venture out without letting someone know where you are going. A good spud bar is paramount for testing the ice but any heavy stick will work. Place your cell phone in a plastic bag, carry a rope along and invest in a reliable ice axe in case you should fall through.

Sources indicate that in most cases, ice anglers like to be mobile, drilling holes in the ice until they find fish. That’s not necessarily a bad practice at the right times, such as mid-day or slow bite periods. However, use your fall fishing as a form of scouting. If you found good weed beds and break lines near shore in September and October, target those same areas the first few days and weeks of ice fishing.

It has been revealed that you need to be stealthy when fishing early ice, because fish may very well be shallow or on the move as they transition into the coldest water temperatures of the year. There are a lot of latest noises, from footsteps to augers, and ATVs coming from above, making these walleye a bit more cautious than usual. Move quietly and minimize noise especially during peak hours such as early morning and evening. Do your best not to move when the fish are moving. As the sun begins to set, you should already have your holes drilled and be fishing at or relatively close to where you expect the fish to be, come evening. Being set up for the fish before they arrive is key to not spooking them out of the area.

Bait size is often overlooked by many ice anglers. But it’s pretty simple. Bigger bait means bigger fish. If you are targeting panfish, make sure you are using small baits such as tungsten jigs and small waxies. If you are targeting eater size walleye, you can often get by with a fathead minnow or shiner on a jig, mid-size spoons, and glide baits will put those walleye onto the ice as well. For trophy walleye don’t be afraid to rig up creek chub, red-tails, and larger profile baits such as Rippin’ Shads, Rippin’ Raps, and many of the other lipless style baits. When the bite gets tough, downsize your baits and minimize expectations. Everyday isn’t a trophy walleye day.

Tip-ups have been around for as long as I can remember and they are a great way to cover water and maximize the number of baits you can legally have out. I prefer to fight the fish on a rod and reel versus the old hand lining method. With all the innovations in ice fishing rods, it is easier now than ever. Placing your rod in a rod holder (known as dead-sticking) is extremely effective and many will tell you that their bigger fish came on these setups. A dead-stick rod allows you to see the bite easier. The rod loads up and in many cases will set the hook for you instead of letting the fish swim around freely while getting tangled up in other lines. And when it comes to fighting big fish, you are more likely to land them on a rod and reel combo as opposed to hand-lining a lunker top side. No transducer is needed in the hole of your dead-stick, which minimizes noise and why many believe bigger fish are more likely to bite.

Recent findings suggest that lively bait can be a challenge when you’re fishing in arctic temperatures. But with all the innovations in insulated and aerated bait stations keeping your water moving and bait highly oxygenated they will remain as lively as they were when you purchased them. It’s usually the angler’s fault for not having lively bait. The cold water temperatures create more viscosity in the water, which means everything moves slower. This is why an active bait can attract a fish to bite from a long distance versus a dead minnow hanging below the ice. Shiners, fatheads, and red-tails are all excellent live baits for ice fishing based on your location. Red-tails are a favorite among Minnesota anglers whereas shiners and fathead minnows, work just about anywhere. Creek chubs are the go to in the Dakotas and when kept fresh and alive they are some of the most active live baits under the ice sure to entice a hungry walleye.

Shorelines are a great starting point during early ice. Most shorelines hold structures such as weeds, rocks, and sand, as well as warmer water initially, making for a great starting point. As the day progresses, look for deeper water nearby such as main lake points and breaks. If you can find a location with a break fairly close to shore this can be the ticket as you won’t need to move a lot throughout the day and you’ll be in the perfect position for when those active walleye move up shallow to feed again.

It has been revealed that weeds hold fish all year long, because they create oxygen, which attracts everything in the food chain. Finding good weeds late in the winter is tough, but early ice weed opportunities can be the ticket. The use of a good underwater camera to do some mid-day scouting for weeds can pay dividends come evening.

Sources indicate that just like your bait, you need the right setup for the technique you initiative on fishing. A soft tip and longer rod can make for a great dead stick. But you will want a more medium to heavy powered extra fast action rod for larger baits when targeting those trophy walleye. The fast action tip will ensure quicker and more solid hook set. A medium action rod will give your bait the proper action when worked vertically through a hole as well as more control over that tanker walleye to guide it up through the narrow ice opening. The right rod will increase your hookups and your ability to land the fish. The wrong rod will increase your odds of missing bites and weak hook sets resulting in lost fish. When your rod is too soft and the action is too slow it’s very difficult to get a good hook set on a fish as all the backbone and strength of the rod are in the lower third near the reel seat. This backbone is what drives the hook home. These lighter and ultralight rods are best suited for panfish. When targeting walleye a longer rod (32-inches), such as a St. Croix CCI Dead Eye, allows the walleye to bite the bait feeling minimal resistance from the rod allowing it time to “load up.” This type of setup is perfect for a “deadstick” allowing the walleye to devour the entire bait before feeling the resistance and in turn self hooking itself.

According to recent reports, as ice anglers, we know the cold well, but far too often anglers are not dressed appropriately. Wintertime temps are seldom stable and in the upper Midwest, you can count on the wind making it much colder than what your weather app forecasted. Once you’re cold, it’s hard to get warm without leaving the ice for a short period of time. Wet hands make it even worse. Packing a small fishing towel can go a long way as well as extra pair of gloves. You will see many seasoned ice anglers overdressed for good reason. It’s much easier to take off a layer than add a layer that you didn’t bring with you. Striker Ice suits has a huge array of floatation suites, bibs, and jackets that also come with many layering options, making them a go-to for ice suits and accessories.

#56505. Latest Update: A Desk Jockey Passed on 40 Brown Bears. The 41st Charged

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4129 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A Desk Jockey Passed on 40 Brown Bears. The 41st Charged

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The 41st Bear,” appeared in the September 1961 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • John Yenter turned away from a 20X spotting scope and looked me right in the eye.
  • According to recent reports, I had just refused to go after the 39th bear that failed to meet my specifications, and John, my hunting partner, was again giving me a piece of his mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The 41st Bear,” appeared in the September 1961 issue of Outdoor Life.

John Yenter turned away from a 20X spotting scope and looked me right in the eye. He remarked, “Bill, you’re absolutely crazy. Forget your foolish specifications and collect that bear. You’re acting like a decrepit old desk hand, not a hunter.”.

According to recent reports, I had just refused to go after the 39th bear that failed to meet my specifications, and John, my hunting partner, was again giving me a piece of his mind. He never uses profanity, but he can do a blistering job without it. He had killed his bear like an expert, and now I, the junior member, was giving him trouble. Being six years older than I am, he felt perfectly justified in straightening me out.

It started months ago back in York, Pennsylvania, where my job — director of purchases for a large manufacturer of air-conditioning equipment — classifies me as a professional desk hand. I guess I look the part — gray, balding, and past several of man’s milestones.

My business associates in Borg-Warner are fond of trying to decide whether I was born a penny-pincher, which made me a purchasing agent, or the other way around. While they were debating that glitch, I was concentrating on a 60-day toughening-up routine of golf, bowling, hiking, and calisthenics to convert my body from paper-shuffling to hunting condition. This was notable because John C. Yenter, a building contractor from Tyrone, Pennsylvania, and I were planning a Kodiak bear hunt. We had so completely enjoyed our polar bear hunt in Norway’s frozen arctic region (“Desk Hand vs. Polar Bear,” Outdoor Life, December, 1957) that John decided his work with West Virginia Pulp & Paper Firm could wait while we took a brown-bear hunt.

It has been revealed that I wrote down some rigid specifications for my trophy brown bear and made a silent vow to live up to them. I wanted a male with a 10-foot-square hide, brown in color, a perfect pelt, and weighing 1,000 pounds or more.

Research indicated that Kodiak Island raised the largest, brownest bears, and a spring hunt would be my best bet for a trophy with a full-grown, unrubbed pelt. The idea was to get a bear fresh out of hibernation — before he ruined his pelt with mating-season fights or started to shed his winter coat. We scheduled our hunt for late April and early May, which appeared to be the prime time for Kodiak brownies.

We met our outfitter, Alf Madsen, in Kodiak Village, on April 27. We knew that most Kodiak bear hunting is done from the salt-water bays around the island, but records show that more massive bears are taken in the interior. So we were bound for Karluk Lake, in the center of the southern part of the island.

In a recent development, the flight up the valleys, around and between the snow-covered mountains, was a sight so beautiful that we almost forgot we were in a little single-engine pontoon plane and at times many miles from any water to sit down on. We were in camp and ready to hunt on the morning of April 28.

Our camp consisted of one frame cabin, one tent cabin, and an outhouse, without door, 100 yards north on the main bear trail. All the camp equipment, including two outboard boats for lake travel, had been flown in.

Recent findings suggest that karluk Lake looked a lot like one of the fjords of Norway. The blue water of the lake was now entirely clear of ice, but there were deep snowdrifts on the mountain peaks above the lake. If we’d never seen a bear, the wild beauty of the place would have repaid me for the trip in full.

We started the hunting campaign with all energy, and in two days we saw and classified 16 bears. I refused to stalk any of them because they failed to meet my specifications. John eventually suggested that I was displaying the stubbornness of a mule, rather than the calm judgment of a purchasing agent.

Sources indicate that our guides were by reputation the best on the island, and they soon proved that they deserved their standing. Some would call them Aleuts, but in reality they were members of the Koniaga Tribe, which has been considerably diluted by the Russians who owned the island until we bought Alaska from Russia in 1867. Our guides were proud of their Russian and Koniaga lineage, but they’re loyal United States citizens.

Recent findings suggest that my guide was Grishka Nicoli, and John’s was Nick Malutin. These guides spoke their native Koniaga language, which is spoken only and not written. They also spoke fluent Russian and awkward English. They spend about three months of the year as hunting guides and four months as commercial salmon fishermen. For the rest of the year they’re Koniaga gentlemen of leisure. Like my hunting partner John Yenter, the guides were convinced that I was entirely too meticulous in my trophy specifications.

It has been revealed that the only encouragement I had came from Kim Clark, who had become a very notable part of our expedition. His full name was Webster Kimberly Clark, and he was a refuge biologist employed by the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Kim had been reared in Greenfield, Massachusetts, had studied at the universities of Michigan, Massachusetts, Missouri, and Yale. He has a Doctor’s degree. Clark had done a vast amount of field research and had become one of the top authorities on North American bears. He was stationed on Kodiak Island by the federal government to study Kodiak bears.

Kim Clark had read my stories in Outdoor Life.* When Kim learned from outfitter Alf Madsen that I was planning a Kodiak hunt, he met me in Kodiak Village and asked if he could join the group to observe and record the data on bears killed. We were glad to have a man of his ability and knowledge.

During the early part of our stay on Karluk Lake, Kim worked alone and permitted us to hunt as hunters, not as scientists. He was a great addition to our expedition, because his lectures at night permitted us to do practical field work the next day in connection with our hunt. Between hunting, field and night classes, we were extremely well occupied.

In a recent development, had it not been for Kim encouraging me to stick to my specifications, I might have given up. He encouraged me because accurate field data on a substantial male brown bear just out of hibernation is apparently very scarce.

By the third day my partner John was adjusting his own specifications to suit the bear that was in sight. We were glassing a brownie on the shoreline across the lake, and through the glasses it looked good — perfect hide, pleasing color, but slightly under my requirements as to size. John wanted it.

In a few minutes we were on our way across the lake, approaching very quietly so as not to alarm the bear. We landed several hundred yards from the bruin, and John started stalking the animal with his guide. In spite of the skill they displayed, the bear caught the man smell. He was on his way up the mountainside before John could shoot. He and Nick stood on the shore watching the occasional motion of a bush which indicated that the bear was going higher and away.

Industry observers note that the bear was 150 yards from the lake shore when he came into a little opening in the brush where we could see him. At that point he made the biggest and last mistake of his life. He stopped and looked back. At that moment John fired. The bear fell. Two more shots finished him completely. John’s performance was a credit to him, to his .375 H. & H. Winchester, Model 70 rifle, and its Bausch & Lomb scope sight.

It was without question a big bear, the color was excellent, the 8½-feet-square hide was prime and perfect. John was a thoroughly happy hunter.

With his bear hide strung up to dry, John concentrated on the wonderful trout fishing near camp, with time out now and then to think up some new criticisms of my ideas about a proper trophy.

At the end of the ninth day we sized up the situation and found that we had glassed 40 bears, killed one. I was still holding out for a bigger and better one.

Industry observers note that the weather was perfect for the first three days, which was probably why we saw so many bears. There was rain every day after that, and visibility was often too poor for good work with binoculars. There’s no climate on Kodiak, just a vast assortment of unexpected and undesirable weather.

According to recent reports, when we started out the 10th morning, we found that what had been rain at the lake camp during the night had been snow above the 1,500-foot level on the mountain. In spite of that, our hunting began early, and at 8:30 we saw a bear that looked very interesting. He was a mile from the lake shore, 1,600 feet higher, just above the new but temporary snow line.

Trying to get a better look at the bear, we moved up the bed of Cottonwood Creek. This took us out of sight of the bruin momentarily, but we knew exactly where he was because the snow line established his elevation and the pass made in the mountains by the creek marked his location the other way. Yet, an hour’s looking from our fresh position failed to locate him.

We then climbed up high on the right bank of Cottonwood Creek, and from there we glassed constantly until noon. We felt sure that the bear was there because we certainly would have seen him if he’d walked away.

At noon we abandoned that position and moved to a spot across the lake, a mile farther away, which gave us a better perspective and a view of more of the ground area. We took turns eating and resting, but we were constantly looking. The rain returned in full force and it was a very uncomfortable situation.

It has been revealed that we never saw a sign of the bear until 4 o’clock, when suddenly he stood up and was in plain view again. It was now evident that we’d first seen him when he finished his morning feeding, and he’d bedded down for the day. Now he was up feeding again.

After a few minutes of careful observation, the guides decided that this bear would meet every point in my specifications. This was a fine display of skill on the part of the guides and is something I could never hope to duplicate. To the inexperienced, a bear two miles away through a 20X Bausch & Lomb telescope is just a bear, but my guide was able to classify him very accurately as to sex, size, and condition.

I knew enough by now to trust this guide’s judgment, and in a few minutes we were on our way back across the lake to start the stalk.

Before we reached the far shore the clouds had dropped so low that the mountains were completely obscured.

Industry observers note that since John had killed his bear, we decided that he’d stay with the boat and the two guides would accompany me on the climb up the mountain. It took a few minutes to strip for action, which meant down to heavy underwear, a sweat shirt, rain suit, and hip boots. This sounds like unusual mountain-climbing equipment, but the first mile of our climb would be accomplished by wading up the creek. It was much easier that way than climbing through the murderous alder thickets on either side.

In a recent development, by 5:30 we’d accomplished the most difficult part of the climb and were at about the same height as the bear and 500 to 800 yards to the right of him. At this point we climbed out of the creek and dived into the alder thicket. All alder thickets are nasty, but this one was the worst that I’d ever seen.

Soon we picked up a prominent bear trail, a path so worn that one of the guides called it “a bear highway.” It was obviously the main bear trail on that particular mountainside, and we felt sure that my bear was on it. We had no idea which way he was traveling, so it was possible that we’d meet him at any moment. It was also possible that he’d park a few yards off the trail to observe and properly take care of anything that might be using the bear highway. It’s this kind of thinking that prevents daydreaming on brown-bear stalks.

Grishka, who was in front of me, explained that he’d lead and watch ahead. Nick would bring up the rear and watch behind us and to the sides of the trail. I was free to watch any angle that suited my fancy. I think this was a polite way of telling me that they didn’t trust my powers of observation.

I was planning what I’d do if certain things happened. I realized that any shooting would be at very close range because of the thick alders and the heavy fog. While my guides were both carrying .348 Winchesters with open sights, I was carrying a .375 Winchester with a Bausch & Lomb scope. No scope is ideal equipment for a quick shot at 10 yards, and I wished for an old-fashioned V notch and front post.

According to recent reports, nick must have been reading my mind. He stated, “Bill, if we meet the bear and you have trouble with your rifle, just throw it down and grab mine. I’ll be right behind you.”.

According to recent reports, nothing could have done me more harm than that speech. I knew now that he had no more confidence in my equipment than I had, and I was scared stiff. I had enough acid in my stomach to pickle a ton of iron castings.

We soon came out into the little open spot on the mountainside that we’d marked as the location of the bear when last seen almost two hours before. This clearing was about 100 feet in each direction — no alders, just dead grass almost knee high. We spent 20 minutes searching the open area and forcing our way into the brush around the edges, trying to pick up a trail or some sign of the bear.

Suddenly my head was gripped by Grishka, a powerful man but only five feet tall. He pulled my head down to his level, slapped his wet face against mine. Pointing to the right, he whispered in my ear, “Bear there. Shoot!”.

According to recent reports, about 75 yards away, through a little opening in the brush, I could see a dark spot. It could have been a bear. As I dropped to one knee, my perfect guide braced his knees to my back to steady my position. His 9X binoculars were tight to his eyes and just above my head as he watched the bear.

When I picked up that brown spot in my 2½X scope, I couldn’t tell whether it was a bear or not. If it was, I couldn’t for the life of me see which way he was pointing.

In a whisper, I asked Grishka, “Which end is the head on?”.

After a full minute’s careful observation through his glasses, he put his mouth to my ear and remarked, “Other end. Shoot!”.

It has been revealed that that concise data from Grishka was fed through my fire-control center down to the trigger finger, and my gun fired. I was so excited I didn’t hear the report of the rifle, nor was I conscious that there was any recoil. But I did hear the bullet hit something, and then a fraction of a second later I knew it was a bear. He roared his complete disapproval of the whole situation.

Then it seemed that the brown bulk went up in the air several feet. An instant later it was on the ground and for a split second was completely still. At that moment I fired my second shot, and the bear’s reaction to that was a quick lunge to the right, toward the alders. I fired my third shot as he disappeared.

Recent findings suggest that grishka had said the first shot was good, but I didn’t see how he could possibly know. The bear had disappeared into the brush just as though he hadn’t been touched.

Both guides were now running as hard as they could to the right — in the same general direction the bear was going when we last saw him. It was quite obvious that they were attempting to get ahead of the bear before he reached the creek bed, which was 600 yards away. I caught them quickly and stayed right with them, not due to any bravery on my part, but simply because it was obviously much safer to stay close to them and their two rifles.

According to recent reports, our travel in the next few minutes was parallel to that of the bear, and we could follow his location by the noise he made. I thought — and hoped — that the amount of noise was due to the fact that he was badly wounded, running blind and knocking brush to one side.

A few seconds later we were on the edge of the creek where we could look down a steep bank to the water 100 feet below. Then I realized that the noise of the bear was not to my left, as it had been, but almost back of me and getting closer. I turned to face the noise. A second later that bear came into sight less than 20 yards away.

It has been revealed that it was the most stirring sight a thrill hunter could ever hope to see. That bear was coming at us at top speed, and it looked as though he knew exactly what he was going to do when he got there.

I slammed the gun to my shoulder and looked at the bear in the scope sight. The contour of the ground was such that I could see the back of his neck, so I selected a spot where the neck joins the shoulders. The crosshairs settled on that spot. I tightened on the trigger, adding pressure and waiting for the recoil.

But the bear rolled dead as Caesar before my rifle went off. I lowered the weapon still cocked and loaded. I never have felt so cheated in all my life. In another 1/10th of a second I could have been the Man Who Stopped the Charging Brownie.

Later examination revealed that the first shot had gone very effectively into his side just back of the ribs, forward under the spine, just grazing it, cutting the main blood vessels just back of the heart. Clearly the bear had been too far gone to make a determined charge. He was only making a blind run with his last spark of life, and we happened to be in his path.

That bear was coming at us at top speed, and it looked as though he knew exactly what he was going to do when he got there.

Industry observers note that I examined the bear closely, and was glad that I’d stuck to my specifications. It was a male, the color dark brown, the hide in perfect condition, and the size was enough to flatter any desk hand. It was the 41st bear we’d seen on this trip.

Suddenly I realized that it was beginning to get dark. We’d have to leave the bear and return the next day to do the skinning. I was worried about what might happen to the hide overnight, but Grishka said, “We leave strong man smell here. Nothing bother.” With a grin he added, “The strongest thing here is white-man smell of your sweat shirt. We leave it.”.

In a recent development, I peeled off the shirt and he tied it to a limb above the bear. When we returned the next morning the shirt and the bear were there and nothing had bothered it.

The guides, Kim Clark, and I left camp early next morning and climbed the mountain to skin the bear. John remained in camp. He and the cook, Pete Unger, had planned a fishing trip.

Kim was keenly interested in the bear from our description so we went in loaded with camera equipment, scales, surgical instruments, test tubes, and specimen bottles. Very few Kodiak bears have ever been accurately weighed and examined, and this is especially true of massive bears just out of hibernation.

According to recent reports, my bear was an ideal specimen for studying the effects of hibernation, because he evidently had just come out of that lethargic state. The stomach was found to be about 1/10 full, and the contents weighed 16 pounds. Carefully separated and weighed, we found that the contents were 55 percent blue-joint grass, 20 percent nettle, 20 percent wild celery, and 5 percent poque, which is a parasitic growth on the roots of the alders. There was no animal matter present.

According to recent reports, the intestine was then examined and the length was accurately determined to be 77 feet 6¾ inches. It was then split from end to end for internal examination. There was no food in it. This indicated two things: first, that the bear had not been out of hibernation long enough for food to pass through the stomach into the intestine, and second, that he had gone into hibernation with the intestine completely empty, which conformed to the generally accepted theory. Further examination revealed there wasn’t a sign of ulcer, scar, scab, or scale in the stomach or intestine.

According to recent reports, we also observed that there were no parasites of any kind in the entire digestive tract. This is one of the strange results of hibernation, because this bear during the six months of feeding eats carrion of all kinds, specializing in dead fish. He also digs up and eats worms, insects, and roots. When winter comes, he’s literally and actually a fur coat full of worms. There are thousands of them, including 10-foot-long tapeworms. The bear knows instinctively that he cannot go into hibernation with any food in his body; it would ferment and cause serious trouble before spring.

Recent findings suggest that so when winter approaches he goes on a bedtime diet of certain plants and berries. Then, after a few days of fasting, he’s completely empty. The worms go with the food, and he goes to sleep physically clean. His stored body fat keeps him going till spring.

Every piece of this bear was carefully weighed. He weighed 840 pounds at the time he was killed. Kim Clark figured his weight when he was fattened for hibernation in the fall would have been about 1,300 pounds.

His age was estimated at ten years. The rough field measurement of the skull indicated a Boone and Crockett rating of 28½, against the world record of slightly above 30 inches. Unless the skull shrinks more than an inch during the drying period that must precede official scoring, the trophy should rate a place on the Boone and Crockett record list. This was in every respect an outstanding bear. I learned a lot from him, and much more from Kim Clark.

It has been revealed that the skull and all the data collected were sent to Dr. Robert Rausch, Arctic Health Research Center, Anchorage, Alaska, where it became a part of their records.

Read Next: We Stalked a Cannibal Brown Bear That Was Trying to Kill a Cub.

According to recent reports, we were glad to work with Dr. Kim Clark and Dr. Rausch, but in a way it was unfortunate. I can’t enlarge on the size of this bear as the years roll on and the hunt becomes a fond memory. This is one Kodiak that will never experience any post-mortem growth.

Industry observers note that *H. L. Consley, who has become known to Outdoor Life readers as the Desk Hand, is the author of “Desk Hand in the Yukon,” in the January, 1956, concern; “Desk Hand Afloat,” November, 1956; “Desk Hand vs. Polar Bear,” December, 1957, and “Desk Hand in the Arctic,” August, 1959.
