#56503. Trophy Deer Hunting Is a Trap

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1050 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Trophy Deer Hunting Is a Trap

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Trophy Trap,” was originally published in the November 2006 problem of Outdoor Life.
  • It has been revealed that it was almost 40 years ago that the first whitetail came into my life.
  • Sources indicate that finally, I had entered the cadre of hunters who had taken a whitetail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Trophy Trap,” was originally published in the November 2006 problem of Outdoor Life.

It has been revealed that it was almost 40 years ago that the first whitetail came into my life. I dropped him on a granite ridge in New York’s Hudson River Valley, where, on a clear day, you could see the Empire State Building 40 miles away. The buck was only a forkhorn, but I was beside myself with excitement.

Sources indicate that finally, I had entered the cadre of hunters who had taken a whitetail. In those days, that feat often took some doing.

Back then, we knew next to nothing about white­tails. I worked as post forester and wildlife biologist for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point for eight years in the late ’60s and early ’70s, and one of my jobs was to manage the hunting program on the academy’s 16,000 acres in southern New York. I recall seeing large scratch marks under trees where some animal had pawed away leaves, but I had no clue what had done it or why. And neither did any­one else I talked to.

Then came newly introduced research as modern wildlife man­agement started to steamroll along, and we learned that those pawed areas were spots that somehow were linked to whitetail bucks before and during the rut. Now we call those disturbed areas “scrapes,” as every whitetail hunter from age 8 to 80 knows. Along with the research came the inevitable desire to “improve” whitetails and grow bucks with bigger and bigger racks. Studies on nutrition and genetics unearthed the means to grow super bucks. Intensive management was suddenly the name of the game around the country. People devel­oped genetically altered monster bucks, put up fences to contain them and began to sell their semen for about as much as my pickup truck cost. Since then breeding has become big business. And in some circles, hunting has become a matter of horn inches rather than the experience itself.

Am I complaining? Not at all. In fact, some good pals of mine run commercial whitetail preserves where intense management produces major racks for their clients. That’s their business. And it’s here to stay. I simply see it as a sad commentary when we focus on the size of the rack rather than the smells, sights, and sounds of a damp oak forest and the raucous cries of jays and crows. Everything in the woods contributes to the total experience — and if a spike or forkhorn buck shows up, then you can be proud to flip off the safety, squeeze the trigger and smile all the way home.

Happily, this major-buck syn­drome hasn’t affected everyone yet. Plenty of hunters, young and old, are still thrilled to down a forkhorn buck, but upcoming management concepts threaten the option of taking younger bucks. Biologically speaking, it’s indeed smart to let the younger bucks in some habitats live another year or two. My problem with the new techniques is that we continue to focus on the size of the antlers.

Industry observers note that proponents of associations that pro­mote minimum antler restrictions steadfastly insist they aren’t focusing on trophy deer. But it seems to me that when you require a deer to be of a cer­tain size before you can shoot it, it’s trophy hunting, pure and simple. Yes, these techniques work in some areas; it just bothers me that we are forced to adhere to those rules. Call me old­fashioned if you like, but I hanker for the good old days.

Read Next: Why Do I Hunt? The Answer to Hunting’s Toughest Question.

I wrote about this subject recently and a reader wrote back and called me a hypocrite. He remarked that I write for OUTDOOR LIFE and that this magazine endorses trophy-buck hunt­ing. Well, hellooooo. Show me a hunting magazine that doesn’t promote big-buck hunting. There aren’t any. Show me a magazine with a forkhorn buck on the cover. There might have been one, once, but I never saw it.

Industry observers note that it’s human nature to appreciate qual­ity. That’s why the Guinness Book of World Records and the Miss America pageant have such appeal. We admire the biggest, the best.

Sources indicate that A hunter who gets a truly big buck, even when it’s total luck, becomes an instant hero. He endorses products, appears in ads, gives seminars and is a big name in hunting circles. The vast majority of these trophy owners just happened to be at the right place at the right time. Most did not “pattern” the buck, watching it for months before the season and discovering what trails it used. The lucky person was simply in the correct tree stand when the buck happened to walk by.

Recent findings suggest that whitetail hunting today is totally for­eign to what it was when I killed my first buck. In much of the country, farm­ing practices and more restrictive hunt­ing produces older bucks with larger antlers. High fences and nutritional supplements aren’t necessary in those places. Pals who live in the Midwest, for example, say that a few decades ago they never saw the likes of the bucks running around now. I’ve been hunting Iowa for years. The size of the bucks showing up these days is scary.

In a recent development, all of us would like to shoot a big buck, myself included. Personally, I have a problem with antlers. When I see them, as long as they’re legal, the rifle is likely to swing up to my shoulder. There are exceptions, such as on a recent hunt in Kansas where I was told all sorts of 150-class bucks were waltzing around. I never saw one. I passed on plenty of other dandy bucks, ended up never firing a shot and cussed myself all the way home. Then there was the time in Saskatchewan, when a buck scoring 162 walked under my stand. It was pure dumb luck. I shot him, and I’m proud of him, and he’s my biggest buck ever, but I’m even more proud of a little six­pointer that hangs next to him.

But that’s another story. As they say, a trophy is in the eye of the beholder. That’s the bottom line.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

In a recent development, A grizzly cub, significant as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

Sources indicate that “Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

In a recent development, I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, major and fast and flat to the ground.

I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

Latest Update: How to Soap-Tan a Rabbit Hide at Home

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1427 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the cold winter months, rabbit hunting is one of my favorite things to do.
  • Rabbit fur is incredibly soft and beautiful when it’s prime, and at the beginning of rabbit season this year I decided to start saving my rabbit hides to eventually make a blanket.
  • I knew that it would take quite a few rabbit pelts to create a blanket for anyone other than a baby, and sending them away to be professionally tanned would cost more than I wanted to spend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the cold winter months, rabbit hunting is one of my favorite things to do. Especially right after a fresh snow—there’s nothing like flinging arrows at cottontails.

Rabbit fur is incredibly soft and beautiful when it’s prime, and at the beginning of rabbit season this year I decided to start saving my rabbit hides to eventually make a blanket.

I knew that it would take quite a few rabbit pelts to create a blanket for anyone other than a baby, and sending them away to be professionally tanned would cost more than I wanted to spend. So, I decided to tan the rabbit hides on my own.

I have tanned several deer hides, squirrels, fox, coyote, and mink. Rabbit, however, is a completely different story. If you’ve ever skinned a cottontail rabbit, you’ll know that their hides are the “tissue paper” of furbearing animals. Their skin is so thin and delicate that you can easily skin them without using a knife.

There are many ways to tan animal hides, and it can be overwhelming. Even once you decide on a specific method, there are various ways to approach it. After several nights of scouring the internet, including many taxidermy sites, I discovered a method called soap tanning that looked like it might work for rabbits. All the instructions I found were vague, but the process seemed simple enough. Not only does this method use simple household items, but it’s free of harsh chemicals. That means it’s safe to do indoors, and with small children and animals around.

Related: How to Butcher a Rabbit.

The whole process, excluding the drying, only took me about an hour from start to finish. It was very simple, and the hide came out beautifully. So, don’t toss those bunny furs next time you bag a few—save and tan them! You can tan the hides fresh, or put them in a Ziploc bag and freeze them until you’re ready to start the process. Thaw 24 hours prior to tanning.

According to recent reports, the first step is probably the most difficult step because, as I noted above, rabbit hide is very thin and tears easily. Most hides are fleshed with a fleshing tool, but that doesn’t work for rabbit hides as it would destroy the thin skin. Working slowly is the best way to avoid tears, but if you do end up tearing the hide, it can be fixed later.

Sources indicate that place the hide fur-side down, flesh-side up on your board. Using the tacks (or nails, like I did) pin the rabbit hide to the board. You’ll want the hide to be taut, but don’t try to stretch it too much. Your hide may be an odd shape, but that’s okay. That will be fixed later, and it’s better to leave it oddly shaped for now.

Sources indicate that once the hide is in place, use the flat side of a butter knife to gently scrape up the layer of flesh from the hide. The flesh will be slightly pink, and the hide underneath will be black and white. Hold the knife horizontal, keeping it as parallel to the hide as much as possible.

Industry observers note that once you’ve scraped enough away, you can grab the flesh with your hands and slowly peel it back from the hide, a little at a time to prevent tearing. Once you do this a few times, this goes fairly swiftly. Be extra careful around holes in the hide that have been left behind from bullets or broadheads.

Once all the flesh has been peeled from the hide, remove the nails from the hide, and remove the hide from the board.

Place the hide in a clean bowl or bucket, and add a cup of olive oil. The measurement isn’t really important; just add enough to saturate the hide. Using your hands, work the oil into the skin side (not the hair) until you see the skin start to turn translucent. Don’t worry if you get oil on the hair side, though, since you’ll wash it in the next step.

In another clean bowl or bucket, add enough room temperature water to submerge the hide completely.

Industry observers note that add a healthy dose of dish soap (I used roughly half of a bottle). Again, measurements aren’t extremely key, you just want a strong ratio of soap to water.

Recent findings suggest that using a large wooden spoon or your hands, gently stir the hide in the soap and water. I started with a spoon and found it easier to use my hands. Be careful not to stir too vigorously, as this will make any holes in the hide even bigger.

Sources indicate that keep stirring the hide until the skin side starts turning white. Once all areas have gone from translucent to white, you’re going to test a small piece.

According to recent reports, do this by bringing a small pot of water to a boil. Trim a small piece of the rabbit hide that’s roughly 2- x ½-inch. (This is a great way to use a ragged edge that you want to trim off to fix the shape.).

Industry observers note that drop it into the pot of boiling water and leave it for approximately 30 seconds. Then use tongs to remove the hide and let it rest on a towel for a second. If the hide curls and is stiff, add more soap to your soap and water solution, and continue stirring. If the hide comes out of the boiling water and is still soft and pliable, your soap tan is complete.

Take your hide out of the soap and water solution, and run it under room-temperature water until all the soap is gone. Gently squeeze the hide to remove as much excess water as possible.

It has been revealed that at this point, you’ll be able to trim the edges of your hide if you so choose. You’ll also want to sew any holes in the hide.

Cut a piece of thread about a foot long. Make a small knot in the one end of your thread, and thread the opposite end through your needle. You’ll want to use a simple whip stitch on the skin side to close the holes. Keep your stitches snug, but not so tight that the skin puckers. The edges of the hole should touch, but not overlap. This will result in smooth fur on the opposite side, with no lumps and bumps.

Industry observers note that this is the longest part of the process. It took roughly 24 hours for the rabbit hide to dry completely. You’ll want to keep it in a dry area, away from pets and make sure no mice or rodents can get to it.

Hanging it on a hook or draping it over a rack so air can get to both the skin and fur side will ensure even drying. The hide will probably shrink a bit as it dries, but this is normal.

You can soften the hide during the drying process, or after. Trying to stretch a rabbit hide just rips it in half, so simply folding it and rolling it into a ball is the easiest way to soften the hide and make it more supple. If you skip this step, however, your hide will still be extremely easy to work with if you are going to use it for a sewing project.

The final step to tanning many hides is to smoke the hide over smoldering coals. Wet hides tend to dry stiff, even if they’ve been worked really well, and the smoke essentially “finishes” the hide in case it were ever to get water on it.

In a recent development, I chose to skip this step, as I blueprint on making a blanket once I have enough pelts, and it’s fairly unlikely that the blanket will ever get wet. On top of that, rabbit hides are so thin that even if they were to stiffen, they would still be very pliable.

If you do choose to smoke your rabbit hide, it only takes about 30 minutes. Keep in mind that smoking will change the color of the hide.

Read Next: Hunting Rabbits is the Perfect Cure for Winter Cabin Fever.

Decide what you want to do with the hide. The possibilities are endless, whether you choose to display the hide on an end table, create fur trim on a garment, or save a dozen to create a pillow or blanket.

#56497. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3157 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures.
  • Recent findings suggest that wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet.
  • Whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures. And as strange as it may sound, bass and deer are really very much alike, at least in the ways they respond to bitter cold weather.

Recent findings suggest that wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet. However, bass do begin exhibiting changed behavior. Generally bass will drift away from the shallows and into deeper water as the thermometer falls because temperatures in the depths remain relatively stable on a day-to-day basis. Here, their metabolisms begin to wind down. The bass, therefore, do not require as much food intake to sustain various bodily functions. Consequently, these two alterations in their lifestyle can make them very tough to catch for all but the most experienced fishermen.

Whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself. Yet few people, aside from biologists, are aware that deer also eat less as extremely cold weather approaches. Chemical changes take place in their bodies, causing their digestive processes to switch to s-l-o-w. This, in turn, allows for the maintenance of various body systems at a greatly reduced rate of food intake.

Another notable point to emphasize about the anatomies of whitetails is that their brains are comparatively small in relation to their overall body sizes. Therefore, the integrated nervous system coursing throughout their bodies is rudimentary at best. As a result, like most wild creatures that do not possess a sophisticated neural apparatus, their pain thresholds are quite high — making them relatively insensitive to bitter cold temperatures. Many hunters are not aware of this because for generations they’ve been led to believe that when the weather goes sour, deer can be expected to do this or that in order “to seek protection from the elements and be more comfortable.”.

In a recent development, body comfort actually has little to do with their changed behavior patterns. After all, the northern boundary of the whitetail’s native range extends more than 150 miles beyond the United States/Canadian border to approximately 52° latitude. Anyone who has lived thereabouts can tell you that winter temperatures frequently average -20°. The wind-chill factor often makes it seem as cold as -75°. Therefore, it just doesn’t stand to reason that animal species such as whitetails would be native to such hostile climes were they not virtually immune to such weather.

We’ve even seen evidence of this immunity right on our southern-Ohio farm where it is not uncommon to experience at least several days of -20° temperatures each winter.

Industry observers note that behind my barn there is an old tractor trail that wends its way through a 40-acre oak forest. Numerous times, while hauling out firewood, I’ve seen deer bedded on nearby slopes. Often they reveal a thick dusting of latest-fallen snow covering their backs — the hollow hairs of their coats providing such superb insulation that their body heat is unable to escape. If I approach too closely, the deer will predictably rise to their feet, shake themselves like soaking-wet dogs and cause clouds of snowflakes to fly — then saunter off to other parts with an air of nonchalance at having been rousted from their beds.

If deer are able to adapt to such gelid temperatures so easily, why is it then, that legions of otherwise knowledgeable hardworking hunters so often strike out when the freeze is on?

Industry observers note that say, for example, that you’ve been hunting in balmy temperatures for several days, have had the opportunity to look over a number of animals but haven’t seen anything you’d really be satisfied with. So you’ve decided to hold out a while longer, hoping you’ll eventually stumble onto “Mr. Substantial.”.

Suddenly, you wake up one morning to the sound of icy sleet pinging against your bedroom window. Bounding from the rack, you are shocked to discover that the wind is whistling a siren song and that overnight the temperature has dropped 35°.

Sources indicate that after sitting on a stand for several hours that morning without seeing a thing, you look and feel like a popsicle. So you begin moving around — sneak hunting — but eventually conclude that the deer have vanished. By day’s end the temperature has fallen another 10°, a light skiff of hoarfrost blankets the ground and your expectations have long since dwindled. You’ve forgotten entirely about taking a nice buck this season and have begun thinking that if you can just manage to fill your doe tag you’ll be very very lucky.

According to recent reports, the scenario is the bane of all hunters living north of the Mason-Dixon Line. Because it’s obvious that the deer couldn’t possibly have just disappeared from the face of the earth, the best prospect for success undoubtedly lies in learning more about their behavioral reactions to severe weather.

According to recent reports, one of the most telling clues to unraveling the mystery of their disappearance can be traced to changes in the whitetails’ body chemistry — the changes that cause them to require less food. Biologists say that this is an annual occurrence and that, like the rut, it is triggered by progressively shorter days and diminished periods of sunlight. Sometime around mid-November, the growth hormone thyroxin, which for the past eight months has been flooding the body, begins dissipating and will remain at a very low level until the following spring.

This shoots down another popular myth about bucks not feeding much during the rut because they are so love struck. Actually, their reduced food intake can be attributed to a conservation measure on the part of nature. In other words, with each additional week of cold weather, food becomes less and less available so nature accordingly reduces the animals’ need for food by enacting significant changes in their body metabolisms.

According to recent reports, hunters should realize that, as the season progresses and as increasing numbers of severe polar blasts begin descending upon their regions, deer can be expected to move around less and less in search of food. The movements they do exhibit are no longer going to be concentrated during the traditional early and late hours of the day but during midday when it is likely to be warmer. Again, the deer are not seeking “comfort” but rather are conserving energy to more efficiently make use of the sharply reduced food supplies.

Industry observers note that I’ve seen this happen with such consistency that I now almost consider it axiomatic. At our northern-Minnesota hunting camp, for example, members of our regular group begin bowhunting in October. We’ve learned from more than 80 years of combined experience that the odds of taking a whitetail early in the season are in our favor if we take up early-morning stands, nap during midday when deer are bedded, then resume our vigils late in the afternoon.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant.

According to recent reports, yet during the final days of the gun season in December, those in our party who still have not scored have entirely reversed their strategies. Now the order of the day, paradoxically perhaps, is to sleep late in the morning, wait on stand during midday, then quit early. There’s just not enough likelihood of seeing anything move — particularly at dawn’s first light — to justify the oftentimes agonizing ordeal of sitting as still as a statue in weather so bitter cold that it gnaws at your innermost fiber.

Industry observers note that of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant. As far as they’re concerned, they want to be in the field every available minute. That’s fine and dandy but, if they want to maximize their chances for success, they should still be willing to make certain adjustments in the way they hunt.

In a recent development, late in the season, and particularly when the freeze is on, they should stillhunt or sneak hunt early and late in the day when deer are most likely to be sequestered in their beds. During midday, hunters should play the waiting game on stand when deer are inclined to be traveling to and from feeding sites.

Sources indicate that but where, exactly, do the deer go when the bottom falls out of the thermometer and ice storms or sheets of wind-driven sleet are lashing the countryside? The three-pronged answer to this is thick cover on a protected south-facing slope in a low-elevation area of terrain.

It has been revealed that two of the most desirable types of thick cover are dense stands of head-high honeysuckle and nearly impenetrable pine plantations. The pines are most often thickets of immature trees that have their whorls of branches close to the ground.

According to recent reports, in the face of adverse weather, deer retreat deep into such seclusions where they can wait out the ensuing tempest. Again, trying to stay warm or achieve some other comfort level has little to do with their evasive behavior. Windy stormy weather makes whitetails extremely restless and nervous. By their very nature, whitetails are already hypertensive and are extremely paranoid creatures. When they’re no longer able to detect, classify and catalog sounds and scents because of the competition from noisy winds and erratic air currents, they waste no time finding a place where they can maintain a low profile. Therefore, rather than allowing themselves to remain vulnerable by bedding on their customary hillside benches and ridgelines, they retreat into deep thick cover. This not only helps to block the wind but perhaps also gives them the feeling that hiding from ready view somewhat compensates for their impaired senses.

Once, for a period of several days in the dead of winter, I had the opportunity to watch an eight-point whitetail buck in a fenced enclosure. This was a wild deer that had recently been captured by biologists for use in various nutrition studies. Its temporary fenced-in home was five acres of relatively open hardwood forest with scattered swatches of second-growth ground cover here and there.

Industry observers note that whenever the weather was warm, sunny and there was no wind, the buck had a particular place it liked to bed. The deer could see in every direction from the high hammock. Yet whenever a frontal storm system moved through the region and the wind began howling, the deer quickly vacated its usual turf. It always went downhill into a little pocket of thick multiflora rose — the only significant cover in the compound — and buried itself right in the middle.

One day as snow clouds scudded against an ominously gray sky and ice-riddled branches creaked in the wind, I watched in amazement as the buck laid on his belly for long hours, his front legs outstretched and his chin resting on the ground. Yet when the wind occasionally intensified with its typical freight-train drone, or an ice-laden branch suddenly crashed to the ground, the buck’s head would instantly come up, swiveling in all directions. Assured that nothing was on the prowl, the buck would then quickly duck back down again. Moments later his head would be up, down, then back up again. Just observing all that nervous energy and pent-up anxiety exhausted me — under these conditions the buck’s entire personality was like a violin string about to snap.

I’m confident that the penned buck would have liked to have had access to much thicker deeper cover to increase his feeling of security. I’m also certain that unconfined deer in their native habitat behave much the same way when the freeze is on. Moreover, a biologist at the research station told me that during one terrible winter storm, the penned buck stayed put for four consecutive days until the weather finally abated.

According to recent reports, in addition to tangled jungles of honeysuckle and conifer forests, whitetails also like to retreat into swamps when the freeze is on. Because of the continually decaying organic matter, swamps are always warmer than other regions and this, coupled with the fact that they’re always found in low-lying terrain, keeps them somewhat sheltered from the brunt of the weather.

However, without meaning to again kick the proverbial dead horse, deer don’t seek out swamps in order to stay warm. They go there because past experience has taught them that they’re not likely to bump into hunters in such forbidding territory and, similarly, a swamp is one place where they can continue to effectively rely upon their senses to forewarn them of impending danger.

Yet no matter what type of cover deer may elect to use for hiding, hunting them when the freeze is on can be extremely difficult because the animals’ minds and senses are so preoccupied with monitoring their immediate surroundings. But there are several tactics that seem to be far more productive than others.

First, of course, pay attention to weather forecasts. Deer seem to have built-in barometers that give them advance notice when hostile weather is about to assault their regions. They take due advantage of this insight by stocking up on groceries, instinctively knowing that once the bitter weather strikes it will preclude safe traveling to and from feeding sites for several days. Then, immediately after the frontal system has passed and calmness again prevails, the deer come out of hiding and return to their favorite food plots. Consequently, stand hunting or sneak hunting — just before and immediately after a storm — are two key strategies no enterprising whitetail hunter can afford to pass up.

Cornfields can be prime places to try because, throughout the Midwest and the northern border states, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing as long as possible. In the past, it was either chopped or combined sometime in October or November. But with storage costs escalating like never before and future market prices uncertain, many farmers nowadays are leaving the corn in the field until such time as they have a specific need for it or until the price increases. Quite often this means as late as February.

Already-picked cornfields are also good bets because a substantial amount of harvest residue may continue to draw deer months after the corn has been combined. On our own cornfields we’re sometimes amazed to see a dozen deer at a time pawing through a foot of snow cover to find spillage.

Sources indicate that I emphasize the importance of finding corn when the freeze is on because native wild foods are becoming more and more sparse with each additional week of winter weather. Other popular agricultural foods such as soybeans are rarely allowed to remain in the field beyond their peak harvest times, so corn is a deer magnet beyond compare.

Hunting during a storm can also pay off. The best opportunity occurs when the temperature does not fall dramatically. This usually means that the wind velocity will not be too fierce and any precipitation is likely to be in the form of huge wet snowflakes that begin clinging to cover like giant globs of cotton candy. Under such conditions, whitetails don’t seem to become as jittery and frantic about their safety and may continue to feed during midday periods. The fluffy snow itself may also pacify them just enough during nonfeeding periods so that they will remain tied to their usual haunts rather than diving headlong into thick security cover.

Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground.

In a recent development, conversely, hunting during the most ravaging freeze-outs offers the least chance of success. Now, patiently waiting on stand is inherently a futile endeavor. The animals simply will not come to you. It is necessary for you to go find them by prowling through swamps, honeysuckle or evergreens.

It has been revealed that never try to approach such cover on level ground. Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground. This will allow you to look down and through the cover and will make it far easier to spot bedded or sneaking deer.

Sources indicate that another option is to round up several pals and begin staging drives, particularly in the case of expansive pine plantations. Here is a unique situation, not unlike hunting rabbits, where the drivers themselves are likely to be awarded as many shots as the hunters placed on stand. The reason, as we briefly touched on earlier, is because deer that have retreated into the catacombs of thick cover are extremely reluctant to expose themselves, to travel great distances or to sever their close ties with that chosen cover where they’ve decided to holeup. As a result, a buck pushed out by a driver may chart a bounding weaving escape flight that actually takes him only a very short distance before he promptly ducks back down to resume hiding.

Read Next: Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck.

Sources indicate that because the drivers are likely to see a good deal of shooting, those hunters placed on stand should use portable tree stands situated as high as practical so they are not in the direct line of fire of their approaching partners. Also — and this cannot be emphasized too strongly — every hunter participating in such a maneuver should be fully clad in fluorescent orange clothing and should maintain loud voice contact so everyone is well aware of each other’s location.

When hunting during freezing stormy weather, wise garment selection also requires careful thought. For sneak hunting or stillhunting, wool is always the best bet because it is noiseless when the fabric grates against brambles and brush. But when toughing out long hours on stand, I rely exclusively upon down-filled duds and bundle up like a snowman.

According to recent reports, I’d be the last to say that hunting deer when the freeze is on is purely enjoyable. Human beings just weren’t designed with bitter-cold weather in mind. But when such conditions prevail, any hunter can indeed fill his tag. Just keep in mind the changed behavior the animals are certain to begin exhibiting and strategy your strategy accordingly.

#56493. Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1108 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like.
  • It has been revealed that it wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change.
  • The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like. When I was a kid, more than 1 million hunters would enter the woods and hunt Pennsylvania’s opening day of rifle season. In my heavily populated area, I always saw a lot more hunters than I did deer.

It has been revealed that it wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change. The deer population was skyrocketing and it hasn’t slowed down. Paired with a decline in the hunting population, I’ve experienced the highest deer numbers of my life recently.

But it’s not just in my area. The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags. Tack on the crazy advancements in technology like cellular trail cameras, the latest crossbows, and even technologically-advanced compound bows, and I truly believe deer hunting has never been easier than right now. Here’s why that’s a good thing — sort of.

Across the whitetail’s range, populations are at an all time high. That’s not just my opinion — it’s fact.

“There are between 30 to 35 million whitetails in the U.S. right now,” says Kip Adams, chief conservation officer for the National Deer Association. “That’s a crazy number of deer on the landscape. And, the harvest data is backing that up. Nationally, we’ve only surpassed three million bucks harvested annually four times in the last century, all of which occurred within the last five years. We also have the best age structure in the last 100 years. So we’re killing more bucks, and older bucks than ever before.”.

The good news here is that the increasing population has been met with increases in opportunity from the tag allocation side, and the harvest data proves those opportunities are working.

“We have expanded seasons across the board, higher bag limits than any point in the last century, and more advanced weapons to fill those tags,” notes Adams. “If you can’t shoot a deer today, you just really aren’t trying very hard.”.

Now, before you go grabbing your pitchforks because you’re still sitting on a pile of tags this season, it’s worth mentioning that Adams and I both agreed that it’s never been easier to kill any deer, but we’re certainly not implying it’s easy to kill a specific deer.

It has been revealed that it’s also worth noting that certain areas across the whitetail’s range have seen a decrease in opportunities as diseases like CWD and EHD have impacted herd numbers, and habitat loss continues with urban expansion. But, for most of the whitetail’s range, opportunities abound.

I’ll be the first to admit I love my cell cameras. I check them almost too often this time of year, but that immediate satisfaction and data grab is addicting. And, that data has helped me dial in the movement patterns of the deer herd in my area based on weather conditions in ways that standard SD card cameras couldn’t. That information, when applied correctly, makes filling a tag substantially easier than just guessing and trying to get lucky.

Sources indicate that take the buck my father tagged last year for example. We had gotten a few photos of him in velvet, keying us in on the area he was using. After planning to stay out of the area and wait for mid to late October when the buck started hitting scrapes, we sat back and waited. Around Oct. 21, we got our first photo of him in the area. And he stayed consistent for three days, hitting the scrape every evening in daylight. On the fourth night, we went in, set up, and a shot opportunity presented itself.

Sure, the stars had to align and the conditions had to be just right for that pattern to exist, but without the technological advancements to trail cameras, I don’t know if we would have gotten a chance at that buck.

In a recent development, tack on the advancements in our gear. From compounds to crossbows, inlines to straight-walls, and even modern cartridge design, we’ve never been better equipped to shoot deer with more accuracy and efficacy.

Recent findings suggest that “Almost all states in the whitetail’s range allow crossbows for everyone now,” Adams says. “Plus, more and more states that used to be shotgun only are now allowing straight-wall cartridges or inline muzzleloaders. All of those additions make it easier for hunters to fill their tags.”.

Industry observers note that while the pros speak for themselves, the cons come down to more of an opinion than anything rooted in fact. I have to wonder what all this ease is doing to the heritage of hunting. Hunting was never about being easy, in fact, I’d argue the opposite. It was about the thrill of the chase, the reward of filling your tag after a long season, putting your woodsmanship to the test and coming out on top, and the conservation of one of America’s most valuable resources.

Recent findings suggest that I grew to love hunting because it was challenging. I was unsuccessful a lot, which put a fire in my belly to learn more, hunt harder, and find a way to be successful through the lessons I learned along the way. I wonder if kids like me are getting the same experience, and what the hook for them might be if not.

According to recent reports, there’s also the ethical dilemma that an easier hunting experience brings. From the ethics and fair-chase argument relating to cellular trail cameras, to the liberal weapon usage and even baiting tactics in certain states, I fear we’re very close to crossing the line into an unfair advantage over our quarry, if we haven’t gotten there already.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

Recent findings suggest that it’s up to us as the hunters, and up to the states to decide how much is too much of a good thing. And as the deer populations continue to expand, I personally don’t see a world where the states are the ones that are going to draw the line. So, this season, as you continue to chase that massive buck or a nice doe for the freezer, ask yourself where you plan to draw the line. And, feel free to join me in wondering how it’s still possible to struggle to fill a tag from time to time.

Breaking: ‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life.
  • It was clear this was the season to try to kill him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer. They kept tabs on the buck with trail cameras and debated when it was time to shoot the high and wide whitetail.

“We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life. “Over last summer when he was still in velvet we saw on cameras that his rack had completely blown up and got huge, with lots of palmation.”.

It was clear this was the season to try to kill him. The brothers hunted hard during a 23-day stint in October, with one of them in a stand every day.

In a recent development, “I was just the lucky one sitting that day when the buck slipped up,” says Zack, a business-studies student at Louisiana Tech University. “My brother, dad, and I put in a lot of work hunting that buck. I would not have taken this deer without their help.”.

The Halberts had multiple setups around their 80-acre hunting property. Zack took the buck from a ground blind on a 48-degree morning in late October.

“The blind faced the woods, and I’m looking one way out a window, then leaned the other way, and there he was at 21 yards,” Zack states. “It’s crazy how you can go from calm and in two seconds go into full panic mode.”.

Sources indicate that zack watched the buck for three long minutes as he waited for a broadside shot. When the buck finally turned, he drew and held at full draw for about 15 seconds. Then he let fly.

The buck took off, and Zack watched where it disappeared into the woods. Then he called his brother, dad, and girlfriend with the news.

It has been revealed that “When I shot I was so pumped I almost shook the ground blind over. Before I got out of the blind I was trying to stop shaking enough to finish my prayer for what a blessing it was.”.

Zack began trailing the deer into timber, but the blood became faint and he decided it would be best to call in a tracking dog.

“I didn’t want to mess up on this deer,” he says.

Tracker Eric Perry and his dog, Blue, arrived that evening.

According to recent reports, “It was getting toward dusk when the dog got there and was put on the buck’s trail,” Zack says. “Blue found it in just 15 minutes. The arrow was a good hit, but there was no exit hole and so not a good blood trail.”.

The deer had died in a creek, and Zack had to wade into the cold water to get his buck out. The crew dragged the deer out of the timber and loaded it into a truck and headed home. Zack estimates it was 5½ years old, and Buckmasters scorer Chris Bates measured Zack’s buck at 205 3/8 inches.

In a recent development, although Buckmasters has a different scoring system than the one used by Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young Clubs (and therefore scores aren’t apples-to-apples), it’s worth noting that the largest nontypical killed with a bow in the state scored, according to P&Y records, 206 5/8 inches. That deer was taken in January 2012 by Alton McLead.

According to recent reports, read Next: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck.

“I know my grandpa Dan, who isn’t with us anymore,” says Zack, “wouldn’t have believed his eyes if he got to see this deer.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road.
  • While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat concerns, the recent development is creating even more consternation.
  • Industry observers note that “It’s unprecedented,” claims Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road. The decision would be part of a push by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority to build a road creating private access to a future mining district focused on copper and zinc deposits.

While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat concerns, the recent development is creating even more consternation.

Industry observers note that “It’s unprecedented,” claims Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. “We’re supposed to allow for balanced use of all of our resources. This would show preference to one resource over another.”.

The proposal, which the Alaska Board of Game will consider during an online meeting Friday, would close 1 mile on either side of the 211-mile proposed road in northern Alaska to all hunting and trapping. It first became public in February and is part of a memorandum of understanding between several Alaskan native corporations and the state. The proposed closure is part of a “subsistence safeguard,” according to a story in the Alaska Beacon. Subsistence hunters could still cross through the road corridor to access other legal hunting grounds.

The hunting and trapping ban would begin July 1, 2029, and remain in place through at least Jan. 1, 2036, regardless of when or even if the road is built, Glaves states.

According to recent reports, the Board of Game considered formalizing the MOU in a July meeting, and opposition was fierce, says Glaves. Still, many Alaskan organizations could not prepare comment because the meeting was in the middle of fishing season. As a result, the board tabled the discussion until its formal meeting in January.

It has been revealed that A few months later, the Alaska Fish and Game commissioner revealed another special meeting Nov. 20 to discuss the project, allowing only written public comment and no oral testimony.

“That isn’t illegal,” Glaves states, “but it’s not in the best interest of engaging the public.”.

Even more importantly, if the closure passes, it tells Alaskans that state public land can be shut down to access at the request of an anticipated industry and with no stated biological need.

Industry observers note that the road has not been built, and there’s some question about whether or not Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democratic governor-elect, will support the project. He has not stated a position publicly but has said he will carefully evaluate money spent by the state. The Industrial Development and Export Authority, an economic development arm of the state, would be responsible for building the road. The Alaska Wilderness League, which opposes the project, estimates it could cost the state more than $2 billion including construction, maintenance, and financing.

The preemptive nature of the closure is particularly troubling to conservation groups.

Read Next: The Ambler Road Project Would Jeopardize One of the Last Great Wilderness Hunts in America.

Industry observers note that “There is no compelling reason to establish these restrictions years before the project is constructed or in the absence of demonstrated need,” she wrote on Nov. 4. “Doing so would also set a troubling precedent of using the Board’s time and public resources to evaluate hypothetical impacts of projects that may never materialize, rather than addressing actual wildlife management and public access concerns as they arise.”.

#56479. The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3818 w)
📖 Baca

The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “I Shot Big Red,” appeared in the January 1967 concern of Outdoor Life.
  • At 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime.
  • Recent findings suggest that I might as well quit, I thought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “I Shot Big Red,” appeared in the January 1967 concern of Outdoor Life. Shelton’s buck is now the 20th biggest typical whitetail ever taken in Kentucky, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. At the time, however, it was the biggest ever taken in Kentucky. It also had a wider inside and outside spread than any deer on the books, including the then-world-record deer.

At 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime. The rain, which had been steady since before dawn, suddenly stopped, and the woods of northern Todd County, Kentucky, were still. I was 20 feet up in a huge sycamore, watching a deer runway that meandered through thick brush. I’d been half-wet most of the day, and I felt another case of chills coming on.

Recent findings suggest that I might as well quit, I thought. I’m not going to see Major Red, and I probably won’t see any other deer.

It has been revealed that my thoughts seemed logical, but another line of reasoning wouldn’t be denied. This was Todd County’s first deer season in modern times, and the season was for this day only. So far as Significant Red was concerned, I had good reason to believe he was the best trophy whitetail buck in North America. Besides, I’m mighty stubborn when it comes to deer hunting. I decided to stay in that tree till dark.

Industry observers note that in front of me, to the north and 30 yards away, a tiny creek flowed through a heavily wooded east-west valley. The runway crossed the creek and continued into dense thickets. I couldn’t see the thickets’ far edge, but I knew the growth thinned against a hillside that topped out alongside a stubble cornfield 200 yards away. The cornfield was 40 yards wide and bordered a little-used gravel road. Across the road was 40 acres of tangled cedars, the thickest cover in the area. I figured any deer leaving those cedars would use the runway I was watching.

Around 2:30 a twig snapped behind me, to the south. Then I heard branches rubbing together and sounds resembling a squirrel digging in the ground. I knew I was listening to a deer.

According to recent reports, the sounds were a few yards off the runway. In another minute they became more distinguishable, and I knew the animal was working toward me. I had two choices: remain motionless in hopes the deer would move past me, or try to inch my way around so I’d face south.

It has been revealed that though the leaves were off the trees, I figured I had an excellent chance of moving without being seen. I was standing on a huge branch, but I was tight against the trunk. Deer don’t normally look up, so I also had that advantage. In addition, I figured the deer was feeding and not alerted to immediate danger. I moved as cautiously as possible.

It took a few minutes to make my move. Now I was facing south. Surprisingly, I could still hear the same sounds, but I couldn’t see any movement.

The sounds kept coming closer. Then, as if by magic, there he was. I saw antlers and legs at the same instant, about 30 yards away. The buck was pawing at acorns. I couldn’t get a clear view of his antlers, and I didn’t dare risk a shot through that thick brush. There wasn’t much I could do except wait.

After what seemed like hours, he suddenly tossed his head up. He seemed to be looking straight at me. His rack was massive, but I knew instantly it didn’t belong to Massive Red. I was sure the buck had caught a glimpse of me or winded me.

According to recent reports, I better take him, I thought. Time is running out.

Sources indicate that my .44 Magnum Ruger carbine was braced against the trunk. I started lining the crosswires of my Weaver scope on his chest. Then, through my variable-power scope, I made an amazing discovery. That buck wasn’t looking up at me at all; he was staring on the level along the runway toward the north.

Now the eight-pointer relaxed and dropped his head to feed again. I heard the same sounds that had startled him. To the north, behind me now, I heard another deer. I glanced over my shoulder and got the second biggest shock of my life. Major Red, in all his glory, was walking toward my tree stand. The monstrous buck was in clear view, 50 yards away and moving down the runway. There was no question about his identity.

Industry observers note that I had seen him two years ago when we had come face to face under the most dramatic conditions. We had startled each other that time. Now I had all the cards. Or did I? I was in no position to shoot. If that buck was alerted to the slightest suspicion, he’d bound into the thickets and disappear.

This dream situation had been in the making for a long time. I guess it really started when I was nine years old, the day I shot my first squirrel. After stalking the gray for hours, I knocked it off a stump with my brother Rudy’s .22. I decided then and there I wanted to become the world’s best hunter. That boyhood ambition has never dimmed, though it’s been realistically tempered by maturity. At that time my family lived in the town of Mayfield, in southwestern Kentucky. There was plenty of small game and birds, but no deer.

By the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

Sources indicate that by the time I was in high school, I was addicted to duck hunting. The area around Mayfield is laced with creeks, rivers, and potholes. It was a duck paradise. I taught myself how to call by sneaking up on flocks of waterfowl and listening to their various calls. I’d go hunting before and after school every day during the season. I practically lived outdoors. But by the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

Sources indicate that I’m 26 now and live in Bowling Green, where I work as a real estate salesman and auctioneer. My wife and I have a daughter, four, and a son, two.

Kentucky’s first modern deer season opened in 1956, when I was still a teenager. I didn’t get a chance to hunt deer until 1959, but nobody ever dreamed about deer hunting more than I did.

In a recent development, looking back, I realize I started my first season as quite a stupid deer hunter. I had no experience, and I’d never seen a deer in my life. The 1959 season lasted three days, and I hunted every one of them from dawn to dark. After it was all over, my record was unblemished: I still hadn’t seen a deer. I’m not sure I even saw a fresh track.

Recent findings suggest that three months before the 1960 season opened, I started scouting my hunting territory on weekends. With six weeks to go, I stepped up my scouting trips to every couple of days. I found runways and beds, examined browse conditions, and located the “use” areas of three herds of whitetails. It all paid off. I killed a fat doe from a tree stand just after dawn on the opening day of the season.

I missed the 1961 season because of a session with Uncle Sam, but I didn’t lose contact with shooting. My ability with a rifle was good enough to win me an instructor’s rating, and I had charge of an army rifle range for 10 months.

Recent findings suggest that in 1962 and 1963, I collected my second and third whitetails. I shot both of them while sneaking silently into bedding areas I’d discovered on scouting trips. My 1962 deer bolted from thick brush 80 yards away, and I dropped him with a single bullet. My third deer, a six-pointer, heard me pussyfooting along, but I saw him before he spotted me. He went down in his tracks.

After I killed my first deer, I studied taxidermy and began mounting deer heads for my friends. I mounted the head of my big six-pointer, but every time I looked at it I dreamed of the day when those six points would be dwarfed by a much larger rack. My dream had plenty of substance because by this time I’d seen Big Red.

In a recent development, we met in October, 1962, while I was living in the town of Elkton, Todd County. I’d heard that the county might be opened to deer hunting, so I started scouting likely areas. I’d done some business with H. Sweeney, a local farmer, and he’d told me he frequently saw deer crossing his fields.

On one of my scouting trips, I found a heavily traveled runway through a hilly area of oak, poplar, hickory, and cedar. The runway was pocked with fresh tracks, and I followed it down through the hills and across a valley to where it led into a rye field. Where the field met the woods, a huge oak tree offered a perfect stand. I decided to climb the tree and see what moved along the runway toward evening.

According to recent reports, about 5 p.m. I heard some deer coming through the woods. It was a warm, quiet day, and the trees were still in full foliage, so I heard them for a long time before I saw them. Shortly, three deer walked below me and went out into the rye field to feed. I watched them for half an hour. Then I heard another deer. He moved steadily to the last bit of cover, then stopped.

Recent findings suggest that I made out the partial outline of a huge deer. The whitetail stood motionless for a full five minutes; then he stepped into the field and joined the other animals. He had an eight-point rack and was the biggest deer I’d ever seen.

Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

Then I heard dogs barking. They were chasing something, and the sounds kept coming closer. A six-point buck suddenly burst out of the woods, ran under my tree, and joined the other deer. As if on signal, they all bolted out of sight.

I never did see the dogs or any more deer, though I stayed in the tree till dusk. I’d traveled farther than I thought, and it was dark before I got halfway back to my car. I decided to bypass the woods and stay in the fields. It was this decision that set up the chance meeting with Significant Red.

In a recent development, I was crossing a fescue field when I approached a man-made stock pond. Banks, about 10 feet high, had been bulldozed around the pond to collect and hold water. I could have walked around the embankment, but I decided to walk along the top of it. A full moon had just cleared the horizon, and the landscape was bathed with an eerie beauty. I went up to the top of the bank and got the shock of my life. Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

Sources indicate that the huge animal was silhouetted against the moon in fantastic beauty. I guess we saw each other in the same instant, and we both froze, each sizing up the other.

Industry observers note that I remember my breath going out in a gasp. My first thought was that I was looking at somebody’s tame elk. Then I knew the animal had to be a deer. His size didn’t awe me so much as did the tremendous spread of his antlers.

We must have stared at each other for seconds. Then the monster buck snorted, whirled, and bolted down the bank and across the field. About 75 yards away, he leaped a five-foot fence. Then he stopped and looked back. I took a few steps toward him, and he trotted into some woods.

I was talking to myself when I got back to the farmer’s yard where I’d parked my car. I went up to the house and knocked on the door. He didn’t seem very impressed when I exclaimed, “I’ve just seen the biggest buck in Kentucky!”.

“That’s Big Red,” he said. “I’ve seen him a few times. You can’t mistake him. He’s a lot bigger than an ordinary deer. His face is sort of reddish. That’s why we call him Big Red. The local farmers know about him, and you’re going to have plenty of company if you figure on hunting that buck.”.

As it turned out, Todd County wasn’t open for deer hunting in 1962 or 1963. Kentucky controls its whitetail population by allowing hunting only in counties where the herds have built up to the carrying capacity of available deer range. In 1956 (the first year that deer hunting had been allowed since 1911) only 27 of the state’s 120 counties were open to shooting. In that season 6,000 hunters killed 1,300 whitetails. By comparison, 14,000 hunters bagged 4,100 deer in 1965. The 1966 population was estimated at well over 50,000 deer, and hunting was allowed in 74 counties.

In a recent development, all of this had its beginning in 1950 when the state began its stocking program with deer bought from Pennsylvania. Original stockings were made in Mammoth Cave National Park and Federal Wildlife refuges. With a ban on hunting, these herds multiplied so rapidly that certain areas became overrun with deer. Live-trapping crews thinned out the overpopulated sections and stocked the deer in other areas that had heavy browse conditions. As these herds build to huntable populations, additional counties are opened to hunting.

In the summer of 1964, the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources announced that Todd County would have its first deer season, a one-day hunt on November 28. I told my brother Rudy about Significant Red, and we planned to hunt him together. We didn’t get much sleep the night before the season opened, and we left for our hunting area at 3 a.m.

A few changes had taken place during the two years since I’d met Significant Red. The monster buck had moved from the Sweeney farm to adjoining woodlands owned by farmer Ross Laster. The deer’s travel routes had also changed, but I knew all about this because I knew Ross well and hadn’t relaxed my scouting trips. I hadn’t seen the buck a second time, but I’d found his tracks many times, and some of the local farmers had seen him just a month earlier.

Dawn was breaking when Rudy and I drove down a gravel road toward Ross’s farm. A mile from our destination, a four-point buck jumped across the road ahead of us, ran to the far edge of a small stubble cornfield and stopped.

“Get your rifle and nail him,” Rudy said as he braked the car.

According to recent reports, “No, you take him,” I answered. Neither of us made a move, and the buck walked slowly out of sight. While we wouldn’t admit it, both Rudy and I weren’t the least bit interested in shooting that buck.

We drove to the farmhouse, and Ross had news.

“That bunch of deer are traveling new runways,” he said. “The best one is about a mile down the road by a cornfield where. . . .”.

According to recent reports, “That’s where we just saw a buck,” I interrupted. “There’s a bunch of cedars across the road.”.

It has been revealed that “That’s the place,” Ross noted. “I’d forget your other looks and pick a couple of stands along that runway.”.

That’s exactly what we did. Half an hour later, I found the big sycamore I mentioned in the beginning. Rudy decided to follow the runway toward some heavily wooded ridges half a mile away.

The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

About 8 o’clock, it started raining hard. By 8:30 I was so wet I went back to the car, changed clothes, and put on a yellow rainsuit. I was almost back to the sycamore when I heard shots from Rudy’s area. I walked up on a ridge and found Rudy all excited.

Sources indicate that “I shot at a buck with a brushpile rack,” he mentioned. “I was curled up under a tree trying to stay dry when I heard a deer coming down the runway behind me. I turned around and we spotted each other at the same time. The buck bolted, and I cut loose with three shots. I lost his tracks right here. He sure was a substantial one!”.

Sources indicate that rudy was a mighty disappointed deer hunter. He’s 35 and one of the best outdoorsmen I know. He’s been a hunting nut all his life, and he taught me how to hunt and fish when I was a boy. He lives in Mayfield where he works as a heavy-equipment operator. He’s married and has two teenage sons.

Rudy went back to his stand, and I stillhunted till noon. We met at the car for lunch, stillhunted another hour, then returned to our stands. It wasn’t long after that when I glanced over my shoulder and saw Big Red.

Sources indicate that I don’t remember any trace of buck fever, but I do recall coldly analyzing the situation. I studied every bit of cover between myself and the deer. About 40 yards from my tree stand, a clump of cedars edged the runway. Substantial Red would have to pass behind that clump. When he did, I’d turn around.

Recent findings suggest that my change in position came off like clockwork. When the animal appeared again he was unsuspicious, and I was in perfect shooting position with my scope lined up on his chest. I decided against squeezing the trigger. I wanted him to come as close as possible.

At the creek 30 yards away, the trophy buck stopped for a drink. The suspense was terrible. I used this moment of his relaxed alertness to suck in a deep breath. The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

In a recent development, suddenly he stopped, turned his head toward his backtrack, tilted his nose, and tested the air. Then he swung his massive antlers forward and walked behind a couple of cedars where he stopped dead still. I had a feeling he was getting nervous.

He might bolt at any second, I thought. As soon as he steps from behind those cedars, I’m going to shoot.

In a recent development, the range was now 25 yards, and there was no question about his increased caution. His face peeked from behind the cedars. Then that unbelievable rack. Again he stood motionless. Suddenly he broke into a fast trot.

The crosswires settled at the base of his neck, and my rifle roared.

It has been revealed that major Red staggered sideways, regained control of his feet, and lunged straight ahead. I aimed my second shot for his shoulder, and the 240-grain bullet spun him around. He dived into thickets alongside the runway and was gone. I heard him crash through brush; then all was silent. I knew he had fallen.

I went down that tree as fast as I could. I got within 30 yards of him, and then he staggered away. I snapped two shots through the thickets, but the bullets never got to him. I heard him fall again about 60 yards to my right. I got within 40 feet of him before he tried getting up. He couldn’t make it. Another bullet finished him instantly.

Industry observers note that I started field-dressing the buck immediately. It wasn’t easy. His bulk was so great I couldn’t move him. I tied his legs to saplings to spread-eagle his hindquarters. Throughout the job, I whistled for Rudy every few minutes. It’s a whistle note we’ve used for woods communication since we were kids. I was nearly done with the chore when Rudy found me. He stayed with the buck while I went to Ross Laster’s farm for help.

Four of the Laster brothers and I got a tractor to within 300 yards of Major Red. Then we had to chop down saplings, clear brush, and cut a fence to get the tractor within 100 yards of the buck. After that it was pure bull work — dragging, hauling, and lifting Big Red till we finally had him balanced on the tractor.

According to recent reports, A few hours later, he weighed 260 pounds on a coal scale. I was surprised because I’d figured he would scale over 300 pounds. I guess the massive antlers fooled me. I was familiar with the Boone and Crockett Club method of scoring trophy deer, and I was certain my buck would score near the top of the record list.

Two months later, the antlers scored 185 4/8 points. My trophy won third place for typical whitetails in the Boone and Crockett Club two-year competition period ending December 31, 1965. Though I didn’t kill a latest world record, I did score some impressive ratings. Substantial Red is the best trophy whitetail ever killed in Kentucky.

Sources indicate that the inside spread of his rack measures 30 2/8 inches, more than 10 inches wider than the current world record. While checking the last listing of all-time Boone and Crockett records, I discovered that this inside measurement is the greatest among all typical whitetail deer recorded there. Though I realize that total score is all that counts, I doubt whether anyone will ever kill a whitetail buck with a wider antler spread than Substantial Red’s.

Sources indicate that read Next: A Son Finally Tracked Down His Dad’s Long-Lost Buck. It’s the Biggest Typical Whitetail Ever Killed in Kansas.

There’s one thing I can guarantee — nobody will ever know a greater hunting thrill than I experienced when I looked over my shoulder in that sycamore and saw the dream of a lifetime coming true.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Industry observers note that outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

Recent findings suggest that and they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

Lessons I Learned from Deer Hunting with My Kids

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
